This series consists of concise books on advanced and state-of-the-art
topics that span the field of biomedical engineering. Each Lecture
covers the fundamental principles in a unified manner, develops
underlying concepts needed for sequential material, and progresses to
more advanced topics and design. The authors selected to write the
Lectures are leading experts on the subject who have extensive
background in theory, application, and design. The series is designed to
meet the demands of the 21st century technology and the rapid
advancements in the all-encompassing field of biomedical engineering.

Preface
Joint replacement using different materials has been in use over the
past 50 years with outstanding success. Millions of people throughout
the world have benefited from total hip arthroplasty THA surgery,
extending their mobility and quality of life by years. However, a clear
conclusion can be the one reported by Kuncická et al. [1] pointing out
that there are opportunities to improve joint replacements by
improving the materials from which they are made. Materials such as
metals, ceramics, and polymers serve critical functions in implant
systems, and therefore their respective roles and properties are
frequently shifting with the advancements in each category and the
introduction of hybrid material systems. After reviewing different
metallic, ceramic, polymeric, and composite materials used nowadays
in THA, there remain issues that must be solved to ensure good pain
relief, increasing more and more the activity levels in young patients
undergoing hip replacement, as well as longevity of the prosthesis,
reaching a higher range of motion as well as stability in those ranges. It
was observed that the mechanical, material, and processing issues are
imperative in the design, selection, and improvement in the fabrication
of hip replacements. For a specific application such as THA, a correct
choice of the defined material to fulfill the requirements of different
standards for a particular total hip arthroplasty system component is
necessary. The proper selection of metallic, ceramic, polymeric, or
composite material plays a crucial role in getting the combination of
properties such as high strength, wear, and corrosion resistance, as well
as biocompatibility. With the passage of time and balancing the pros
and cons of the various materials used for applications in THA, it could
be determined that the use of ceramic materials (alumina matrix
composite mainly) is best suited as bearing material for example.
   In conclusion, the innovations in the design and fabrication
processes for the different materials for THA are raising the great
reality of being able to obtain, in the medium term, implants with
improved performance to match both the biocompatibility and
mechanical complexity of the hip implants. However, to achieve this,
surgeons in close alliance with biologists and engineers cannot be
ignored. They must be persuaded of the long-term durability and

reliability of the available biomaterials. Everything mentioned leads to
the future to see novel biomaterials being developed that will increase
the lifespan of orthopedic implants. Today it is not possible to fully
ensure which material is the one that will dominate orthopedics.

Today, the trend in biomaterials for total hip arthroplasty is designed to
tailor properties and fabricate hybrid materials to achieve excellent
performance metrics in one product.
   Metals and ceramics are considered as biomaterials and being the
central enablers of joint replacement technology in the orthopaedic
field [1] without demerit the use of polymeric materials in some cases.
The specific field of biomaterials has been considered and recognised
as a separate entity since the first meeting held on biomaterials at
Clemson University, South Carolina in 1969, and continues to receive
substantial attention, exploiting the latest technologies in order to
improve the quality of life and longevity of human beings [2–4]. The
high performance of orthopaedic replacements is highly related with

their relative motion via sliding and highly localised loads, where the
wear and surface properties of both metals and ceramics are of utmost
importance [5]. In reason of this, nowadays, orthopaedic implants with
artificial biomaterials have allowed surgeons to ameliorate the lives of
patients by reducing the pain [6] and restoring function to otherwise
functionally compromised structures. The body parts most frequently
replaced in the orthopaedic field are hip, knee, shoulder and spine [7],
replacements for which are currently manufactured from metals like
stainless steel (SS), titanium alloys, cobalt-based alloys and ceramics
such as alumina (Al2O3) and zirconia (ZrO2), or alternatively, a
combination of these. However, in the case of metals, these have
demonstrated strong tendencies of failure after long-term use, thus
recommending the need for revision as a consequence of adverse local
tissure reaction to metal debris, infection, instability, pain, aseptic
loosening, and fracture, amongst others [8]. On the other hand, in spite
of the advantages of the ceramic materials such as their inertness and
desirable mechanical properties, such as high strength, elastic modulus,
and hardness, as well as their excellent corrosion resistance,
biocompatibility, low friction, high wear resistance, and stability in a
physiological environment [6], ceramics have been found to be
associated with some mechanical failure [9, 10]. Taking into account
the advancement in medical technology, it has become necessary to
develop implants with high performance and superior longevity and
biocompatibility, serving a much longer period without failure or
revision surgery with the aim to satisfy the increased population of
active young adults traumatised by different circumstances, so
generating more comfortable living conditions. This was finally
achieved with the latest generation of ceramics for THA, the alumina
matrix composite with the brand name BIOLOX® delta (CeramTec
GmbH, Plochingen, Germany) which was introduced in the market in
2003.
   Excellent reviews and original articles summarising aspects of
metals and ceramics for different biomedical applications, including
aspects related with orthopaedic implants, already exist.
Notwithstanding the foregoing, in this review the authors emphasise a
comparison between the advantages and disadvantages when both
metals and ceramics are used in orthopaedic surgery, showing the

evolution of these replacements provided by advances in technology
and materials [11–14]. This review article, focussed on orthopaedic
implants like hips and knees only, is divided into ten sections, starting
with the state of the art in orthopaedic implants and their
biocompatibility, the requirements to be fulfilled by metals and
ceramics to be applied in the manufacture of orthopaedic implants, and
the limitations and mechanical aspects of these biomaterials. The
review ends looking at the horizons in materials and technologies as
well as the prospects for different materials used for both temporary
and permanent implants in the more used orthopaedic replacements.

2. State of the Art in Orthopaedic Implants

The orthopaedic implants history goes back to the nineteenth century when
the first ever implantation of a large human joint was performed in 1890 [1,
2], and the first total knee endoprosthesis was made of ivory and anchored to
the bones using nickel-coated nails and a mixture of gypsum, resin and
pumice [1, 3]. Implantation of metal-based joint prostheses began in the early
1930s with the first stainless steel total hip replacement (THR), implanted in
1938, being made of the ‘‘vanadium steel” purposely designed to be used
within a human organism [4], but having inadequate biocompatibility and
corrosion resistance. At present, in orthopaedic surgery, the metals more
commonly used and of long tradition for joint replacements are stainless
steels, cobalt-chromium alloys, titanium alloys and to a lesser extent,
tantalum and its alloys, and niobium and zirconium alloys [3, 5]. These metals
remain favourites owing to their good biocompatibility and their ability to
undergo large plastic deformations prior to failure. Despite the above, severe
limiting factors still exist for steels and Co-based alloys including fatigue of

acetabular components in hip join implants leading, inevitably, to loosening of
the implant [3, 6]. Indeed, with the increasing use of THR in younger and
more active patients where revision rates are higher [7–9], new materials
with enhanced properties or the improvement of existing ones is required.
The in-situ degradation of metal-alloy implants is especially undesirable since
this process may decrease the structural integrity of the implant producing an
adverse biological reaction in the host leading to periprosthetic bone loss
[10]. Furthermore, many authors have reported increased concentrations of
local and systemic trace metals associated with metal implants [11–15]. This
implies in depth studies to achieve the right balance between the implant
material and its mechanical aspects, biocompatibility, high corrosion and
wear resistance, and enhanced osseointegration taking into account the three
main combinations of femoral head and acetabular bearing surface materials
as follows: (i) metal-on-polyethylene (MoP), (ii) ceramic-on-polyethylene
(CoP), (iii) ceramic-on-ceramic (CoC), highlighting that metal-on-metal (MoM)
and the combination of ceramic-on-metal (CoM) implants are uncommon
[16]. The material has to guarantee the optimal performance of the
orthopaedic implant without rejection to reach lower revision rates of hip
arthroplasties, mainly in the younger populations, emphasising that this is
one of the most common surgical procedures performed worldwide
estimating, for example, that 2.5 million people are living with a hip
replacement in the USA where the main indications to elect this procedure are
pain and functional limitations owing to osteoarthritis [17, 18]. Additionally,
in Korea, the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service registered that
more than 60,000 THAs were performed between 2010 and 2017, with an
increase of more procedures over time [19]. In this context, new aspects such
as bearing materials and fixation methods, along with new designs of
implants, have been improved in order to return a patient to the activities of
daily living and range of motion in the absence of pain [20].
    Currently, the metallic biomedical materials used in orthopaedics and
their limitations have resulted in improvements to the existing group of
metals and the introduction in this field of ceramic materials, which will be
mentioned later on. The strict use of metals in THA, that is, MoM bearings,
were initially made using large head diameters during 1955–1965 [21]. Their
use declined for some years in the 1970s when Sir John Charnley introduced a
THA device based on MoP made-up of a small metal head and a cemented
polyethylene (PE) cup [22]. Sadly, the concerns about the role of PE wear
particles in osteolysis and loosening were increased with the increasing use of
THA in younger and more active patients, leading to the revision rate
becoming higher [23].

It is well known that stainless steel was the first class of alloy introduced
for orthopaedic implants [20, 24], but independent of its ease in
manufacturing and low cost, and due to its inevitable corrosion, it must only
be used for short duration purposes [25]. Nevertheless, despite stainless steel
being renowned as a biomaterial, it is important to stress that from the many
grades in the stainless steel family, the austenitic 316L stainless steel is the
only category that is used for bioimplant applications given that is favoured
for its inexpensiveness, lack of ferromagnetism, exhibiting an excellent
toughness, even down to cryogenic temperatures, and shows good
biocompatibility according to cytotoxicity evaluation standards [26–31]. On
the other hand, the mechanical properties of stainless steel can be controlled
in a wide range which allows for the manufacture of products with optimal
ductility and strength for different medical uses [30], guaranteeing a
satisfactory mechanical performance as the material can bear significant
loads and experience sufficient plastic deformation before failure, according
to reports by Breme et al. [29] and Chen and Thouas [1]. However, and
considering some controversial reports [32] evoking tremendous scientific
interests in the fabrication of bioimplants which uses large quantities of this
metal (approximately 10 to 20% in the market), in reality the mechanical
working conditions inside a living body differ greatly from the external
environment and stainless steel in THA is typically subjected to fatigue
damage as its fatigue strength is relatively low [33–35]. In this scenario, and
also taking into account its inevitable corrosion, stainless steel is now mainly
being used in short-term implant devices although stainless steel devices
remain available in other countries (particularly the United Kingdom) [20],
but its applications are centred mainly in fracture plates, screws and nails,
emphasising that tibial components of knee prostheses may also be
manufactured from this steel [36].
    Parallel with the use of stainless steel implants and owing to its superior
mechanical properties and corrosion resistance when compared to other
materials used at that time, the development of cobalt alloys began [1] with
the first Co-based alloy implant being introduced in 1939 [4, 37]. Although
the first successful implantation of a metal-on-metal hip joint replacement
with this CoCr alloy was in the 1950s [38], the MoM implants tend to loosen
from the bone despite continuous development and numerous technological
improvements. Both 316L SS and Cr–Co alloys possess a much higher
modulus than bone which in turn leads to insufficient stress transfer to the
bone causing bone resorption and loosening of the implant after some years
of implantation [6]. Knowing that major alloying compositions such as Co, Cr,
Mo and Ni are catalogued as essential trace elements in the human body,

undoubtedly they would be biologically toxic when in excessive amounts
resulting in damaging to the kidneys, liver, lungs and blood cells [39–43].
Thus, the release of particles or ions caused by fretting corrosion, wear, and
fatigue or loosening of the implant, is a big concern for Co-alloy biomaterials
[1]. For this reason, some alloys, especially those with Ni, should be avoided in
applications experiencing hard contacts and friction loading. On the other
hand, the high costs involved in manufacturing have put Co-based alloys at
another disadvantage when it comes to the medical market and although
imperfect, cobalt alloys remain as a favourite metallic implant material in THA
procedures [31]. In spite of the disadvantages, the main interest for these Co-
alloys is not to design new chemical compositions, but to improve the
mechanical properties and performance of the existing alloys by
implementing new and novel processing technologies and thermo-mechanical
treatments, as is the case of the Co–Cr–Mo ATSM F75 alloy which has been
fabricated following a new technology ensuring enhanced wear resistance
and fatigue strength [38]. Nowadays, Co–Cr–Mo alloys are being used along
with cross-linked ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) to
reduce corrosion and wear [44]. Nevertheless, fabrication and finishing
treatments of these alloys have to be processed carefully in order to avoid the
unintentional reduction of one property at the expense of another [38].
   Independent of the above mentioned stainless steel and Co-alloys and the
tendency of these metal-on-metal orthopaedic implants to loosen from the
bone, despite continuous development and numerous technological
improvements, Niinomi [45] reported that the natural selection of titanium-
based alloys for implantation, collects a combination of outstanding
characteristics such as high strength, low density (approximately 60% of the
density of iron and nearly half of the density of cobalt), high immunity to
corrosion, complete inertness to the body environment, enhanced
biocompatibility, low modulus and a high capacity to join with bone and other
tissues [45]. Thus, currently, titanium and its alloys are the most popular
metallic implant biomaterials used in THA, and Ti-6Al-4 V is the most
commonly used alloy for stem and acetabular cementless components of THA
[46]. Undoubtedly, titanium is superior in specific strength and has low
fatigue strength, but is inferior in tribological properties compared with
stainless steels and cobalt–chromium alloys, and therefore its use has
increased over the past two decades because of its lower modulus, higher
corrosion resistance, and better biocompatibility than both stainless steels
and cobalt-based alloys [1]. However, we must not lose sight that the toxicity
of vanadium has led to the development of various vanadium free Ti-6Al-4 V
compositions for applications such as femoral stems and fracture fixation

plates where the Ti-Mo-Zr-Fe alloy is a clear example of that being practically
applied for hip joint stems [1, 47]. Making a comparison of the advantages,
disadvantages, and different medical applications using α, near α, α–β and β Ti
alloys [48], a mechanically reliable titanium alloy orthopaedic implant has yet
to become a reality.
    Metallic materials have predominated in orthopaedic surgery including
temporary devices (e.g. bone plates, pins, and screws) and permanent
implants (e.g. total joint replacements) [49], but only a few are capable of
long-term success as an implant material. In fact, these metals are commonly
categorised based on the major alloying element such as (i) stainless steels,
(ii) cobalt-based alloys, (iii) titanium-based alloys and (iv) miscellaneous
others that include NiTi and alloys of Mg and Ta [50]. Those medical implants
made with this last group of metallic alloys are not yet FDA approved owing to
the significant issues associated with biocompatibility [51] which is, by far,
the main requirement for clinical application of any biomedical implants.
   Steinberg DR and Steinberg ME [52] illustrated the use of ceramics in
arthroplasty during the past century and the explosive growth in the
application of biomaterials in joint replacement during the past 50 years,
which turned out to be the most successful surgical procedure of the
twentieth century [9]. Of course ceramic materials have been integral to this
evolution [53] and they were first considered for use as prostheses in the
1920s, but presenting a lack of sufficient strength and toughness to withstand
the acetabular loads, and many fractured in vivo [54]. Nevertheless, and in
spite of the problems, orthopaedists returned to ceramics because of
favourable properties such as biocompatibility, hardness, wear, and lately, by
the corrosion resistance. During this period, alumina, hydroxyapatite,
zirconia, ceramic-coated metals and zirconia-toughened alumina proliferated
for applications in orthopaedic implants, taking advantage of their inertness
and desirable mechanical properties, as they possess high compressive
strength, elastic modulus, hardness, and stability in a physiological
environment [44, 55]. Ceramics used in orthopaedic surgery are classified as
bioactive or inert according to the tissue response when implanted in an
osseous environment. When the ceramic is inert, it merely elicits a minor
fibrous reaction when it is used as bearings in total joint replacements.
Conversely, when the ceramic is catalogued as bioactive, it is employed as a
coating to enhance the fixation of a device, or as bone-graft substitute because
of its osteoconductive properties [56]. The clinical experience has shown that
ceramic bearing couples can significantly reduce particle induced osteolysis
(i.e. an alumina head articulating against an alumina cup insert offers a
proven solution to the problem of particle induced osteolysis by their very

minor wear rate of under 0.005 mm per year) and the need for revision [57].
It is important to note that the most successful uses of ceramics in
orthopaedics and traumatology is in the use of femoral heads and acetabular
components where particularly, the hardness, and therefore the wear and
scratch resistance of alumina and its composites has been clinically proven.
    Alternatively, zirconia ceramics were introduced in the manufacture of
femoral heads for total hip replacements because of their better mechanical
strength and toughness when compared to alumina [56, 57]. Approximately
twenty years ago, Mg-PSZ ceramic (partially stabilised zirconia with magnesia
as a stabiliser) was the very first zirconia approved by the American Food and
Drug Administration (FDA). Subsequently, Mg-PSZ was replaced by Y-TZP
(tetragonal polycrystalline zirconia which is stabilised by yttria) owing to its
better mechanical strength. However, problems in the clinical use of zirconia
heads related to its lack of phase stability under hydrothermal conditions [58,
59] have led to high revision rates [60]. It is worth remarking that friction in
the hip joints results in a not insignificant temperature increase. Nevertheless,
Lu and McKellop [61] reported an increase in the temperature of the wear
couple zirconia/polyethylene compared with that of alumina/polyethylene
due to the poor thermal conductivity of zirconia. Considering this
inconvenience, the failure risk of zirconia is high and as such the wear couple
zirconia/zirconia has not been introduced in THA [53, 62–64].
   After the zirconia failure, the development of ceramics for THA moved to
alumina matrix ceramic composites as the zirconia-toughened alumina (ZTA)
involving the combination of the attractive properties of both alumina and
zirconia where alumina offers hardness, wear resistance, and phase stability
while zirconia offers attractive fracture toughness. As a result of this, several
research projects aimed to develop a suitable ZTA material for THA, such as
Toni's team [65, 66]. The first ZTA for THA was introduced by CeramTec with
the brand name BIOLOX®delta, which is today considered the gold standard
bearing material for THA.
   Even if the market is led by a ZTA material produced by a single
manufacturer, it is worth mentioning that there are diverse manufacturers for
femoral heads and cup inserts for use in THA, as well as package leaflets and
instructions that contain information about which implants and combinations
are approved. Therefore, if an application or combination of components have
been permitted, then research reports on the functional efficiency on which
the decision to release the combination was approved, will exist. Based on the
latter, it is of paramount importance keep in mind and according to a report
by Willmann [57] that if a surgeon combines components which are not
explicitly approved, then he becomes fully accountable, in accordance with

medical product legislation (MPG), for quality assurance. Moreover, the
surgeon is neither trained nor does he have the equipment to prove his case
considering that there are no technical investigations in existence which could
serve as the basis for approval certification. On the other hand, it is of
paramount importance keeping in mind that combinations of components
from different manufacturers are not approved. Therefore, the
recommendation is never to be mixed and matched. Today, with the
achievements in the performance of the ZTA ceramic parts for THA, the
disclosure by Willmann [57] remains in force. Besides this, it is important to
mention that the scientific community of ceramic materials is studying the
non-oxide ceramic Si3N4 for a potential application in orthopaedics. Similar to
Al2O3, Si3N4 exists as an irreversibly stable phase at room temperature [53],
with a unique microstructure composed of asymmetric needle-like
interlocking grains surrounded by a thin (<2 nm) refractory grain-boundary
glass [67] that provides a strength of about 1000–1200 MPa. This ceramic can
also be applied as a wear resistant coating using physical vapour deposition
(PVD) or chemical vapour deposition (CVD) methods [68–71] and is being
considered, thus far, for both bulk and metal-coated orthopaedic applications.
However, materials scientists, engineers and surgeons are performing R&D to
improve the design, processing, comfort of handling etc. of currently used
materials to solve a great challenge. As a result of this, the first CoC
resurfacing systems made by BIOLOX®delta have been recently implanted in
patients. A summary of diverse metallic compositions used in the
manufacture of orthopaedic prostheses and their properties are shown in

3. Biocompatibility

Armando Reyes Rojas1     , Alfredo Aguilar Elguezabal2,
Alessandro Alan Porporati3, 4, Miguel Bocanegra Bernal5 and
Hilda Esperanza Esparza Ponce6
(1) Laboratorio Nacional de Nanotecnologia, Centro de Investigación
    en Materiales Avanzados S.C., Chihuahua, Mexico
(2) Laboratorio Nacional de Nanotecnologia, Centro de Investigación
    en Materiales Avanzados S.C., Chihuahua, Mexico
(3) Medical Products Division, CeramTec GmbH, Plochingen, Germany
(4) Department of Engineering and Architecture, University of Trieste,
     Trieste, Italy
(5) Laboratorio Nacional de Nanotecnologia, Centro de Investigación
    en Materiales Avanzados S.C., Chihuahua, Mexico

It is well known that the insertion of either a metallic and ceramic
implant or its combination in a bone undoubtedly leads to a change in
biomechanical environment, thus altering the stresses and strains
applied to the bone. It is very important to stress that the
incompatibility of materials may result in interface and mechanical
failure, generating particulate debris, subsequent osteolysis and
implant failure. In defining implant biocompatibility, it is of paramount
importance to consider the biological response both to an altered
mechanical environment and to the liberation of particulate debris.
     It is well known that the common feature of the different metals and
ceramics used in orthopaedic implants (see Tables 2.​1 and 2.​3) is their
intimate contact with the living body. In materials science they are

usually denominated as biomaterials, materials that are biocompatible.
These may be natural or man-made and are used to replace, or assist,
part of an organ or tissue. The prefix ‘‘bio’’ of biomaterials refers to
‘‘biocompatible’’ rather than ‘‘biological’’ or ‘‘biomedical’’ as is often
misunderstood according to a report by Chen and Thouas [1].
   Important investigations by Williams [2–4] suggest that the
implanted material does not cause any harmful effects and that the
biocompatibility must cover all aspects of bio-device function, including
the interaction of cells and tissues with the implanted metal or ceramic
biomaterials. In fact, the requirements for biocompatibility of a
material are very strict and can depend on any specific medical
application. For instance, the rejection of an orthopaedic implant due to
the toxic release of metallic ions will clearly lead to ultimate failure [1].
In this context, a material used satisfactorily in orthopaedic surgery
may, however, be inappropriate for cardiovascular applications because
of its thrombogenic properties [5]. Some studies [6, 7] classify the
biocompatibility of biomaterials according to their ability to induce cell
or tissue death (cytotoxicity), cancer formation (carcinogenicity), to
genetic damage (mutagenicity), immune responses (pyrogenicity and
allergenicity), or blood clotting (thrombogenicity) [5]. Thus,
considering all of these types of biocompatibility problems, a clear and
universally prevalent definition of biocompatibility has been provided
by the FDA [8], to the effect that the material induces no measurable
harm to the host. The important advancements in medical technology
make it necessary to develop metallic and ceramic implants with
superior longevity and biocompatibility, without failure or revision
surgery, in order to address the increased population of active young
adults traumatised by sports injuries, exertive exercise habits, or road
accidents, so granting more comfortable living conditions [9].
Nevertheless, small chemical changes in the surface of the implants
could determine the difference between a device being bio-friendly and
one that is rejected, which may lead to an alarmingly high number of
failures [10].
   Indeed, the biocompatibility of an articulation needs to include an
assessment of the toxicity of fine wear particles while arthrodesis
devices need to be checked for fibrous tissue formation and
pseudarthrosis. Based on this [11], ceramics and ceramic coatings do

have bio-compatibility advantages over their metal and plastic
counterparts. For instance, Warashina et al. [12] performed direct in
vivo comparisons of Al2O3, ZrO2, Ti-6Al-4 V, and high-density
polyethylene (HDP) particles implanted adjacent to murine calvarial
bone, the four tested materials being biocompatible in accordance with
the ISO standard. The osteolytic lesions with significantly greater levels
of proinflammatory cytokines, induced by particles of HDP and Ti-6Al-
4 V, were three-times higher than the ceramic materials, therefore, the
biologic reactivity of the ceramics is lower. There are probably no truly
bioinert substances [13] due to physicochemical changes occurring on
all materials in contact with human tissue. Historically, two
components are part of a THA or articulation of a human hip: a cup
type and a long femoral type element, and these can be manufactured
from metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites. An analysis
demonstrates that polymeric materials alone are too weak and
therefore, not suitable to meet the requirement of stress deformation
responses in THA components. The metals possess good mechanical
properties but poor biocompatibility causing eventual failure, which
may lead to removal of the implants. On the other hand, the ceramics
have generally good biocompatibility but poor fracture toughness and
tend to be brittle. According to the above mentioned, in order to reach
high biocompatibility in combination with mechanical strength and
toughness, composite materials with engineered interfaces are the
focus of many current studies [14–16].
   Besides the interaction of a living system or tissue with a finished
orthopaedic device or its component materials, biomechanical
compatibility is required and therefore, the response of a biomaterial
ceramic or metal to the repeated cyclic load is determined by the
fatigue strength of the material, which in turn determines the long-term
success of the implant. Conversely, the biomechanical incompatibility is
determined by the fracture produced in an implant as a consequence of
an inadequate strength, or a mismatch in the mechanical property
(known as modulus) between the bone and the implant [14, 17, 18].
Hence, the biomaterial used for an orthopaedic implant should be
biomechanically compatible and expected to have a modulus equivalent
to that of bone to guarantee success. A biomechanical incompatibility
can lead to death of the bone cells, commonly known as “stress

shielding”. If the implanted material has a higher stiffness than the
bone, this prevents the required stress being transferred to the adjacent
bone resulting in bone resorption around the implant which,
consequently, leads to implant loosening. Having said that, in
orthopaedic implants the best option is to use a material (metal,
ceramic or composite) with an excellent combination of high strength
and low modulus, close to bone, to avoid loosening of the implants and
a longer service period to avoid repeated surgery, and which does not
harm the patient [19]. Viceconti et al. [20] reported that the surface
chemistry, roughness, and topography of the implant material play a
major role in the development of good osseointegration and it is highly
essential for the implant to integrate well with the adjacent bone.
During THA, both the femoral and acetabular bearing surfaces are
surgically replaced with metallic, polymeric, and/or ceramic
components, and thus many different combinations of these materials
have been proposed with the purpose to examine the performance of
the orthopaedic implant. A high concentration of particulate debris
generated from articulating surfaces clearly initiates a cascade of
adverse tissue response leading to osteolysis, and in certain cases,
loosening of the components. In regard to this, it is important to reach
the optimum combination of materials to extend the longevity of the
orthopaedic replacement and improving the wear behaviour. The
ongoing research in the orthopaedic community is achieving successful
implant-to-body integration [21]. The general requirements of
biomaterials and the problems occurring due to non-compliance are
summarised in Table 3.1 [14].

Metals have been used extensively in the manufacturing of orthopedic
implants for different application in multiple forms. Different materials
throughout history have been tested as replacements for bone. The
extensive use in modern times of metals and alloys is related to the
availability and success at the beginning of the 20th century of several
different alloys using the noble metals. Currently, implants made from
iron, cobalt, chromium, titanium, and tantalum are commonly used.
   The orthopaedic implant market is expected to grow due to the
rising demands for orthopaedic implant procedures in a universally
ageing civilisation. Nowadays, applicable artificial implants can be in
the form of plates, rods, screws, or scaffolds (a porous structure used to
substitute missing osseous tissue). Likewise, there are materials such

as metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites available to fabricate
artificial implants, but due to the complexity of the human skeleton, no
one class of materials is suited for all applications [1]. Materials used
for implant applications should have good mechanical strength, high
chemical stability, excellent corrosion resistance and biocompatibility
[2, 3]. The metallic materials have predominated in orthopaedic
surgery, playing a major role in most orthopaedic devices, including
temporary devices (e.g. bone plates, pins, and screws) as well as
permanent implants (THA). Despite the large number of metals and
alloys able to be produced in industry, only a few are biocompatible and
capable of long-term success as an implant material where they must
remain stable in vivo for >10 years. The metallic materials that have
been used, or are being researched, for bearing surfaces in THA and
TKA belong to the following classes.

4.1 Stainless Steels
Stainless steel is the generic name for a number of iron-based alloys
that contain a high percentage (11–30 wt.%) of chromium [4, 5] and
can be characterised by their chemical compositions (chromium type
and chromium-nickel type steels) as well as their microstructures [4,
6]. Stainless steels can also be martensitic, ferritic, austenitic, or duplex
(austenitic plus ferritic) [5, 6]. For instance, martensitic steels are
commonly used to produce surgical and dental instruments, while
austenitic steels are suitable for permanent and long-term surgical
implants and joint replacements, taking advantage of their fcc crystal
structure which makes them non-ferromagnetic and possess good
corrosion resistance [7]. The most widely used stainless steel,
denominated as 316 (ATSM F138), can have its designation
supplemented with the letters ‘‘L” and ‘‘V”, where ‘‘L” stands for low
carbon content, while the vacuum under which the steel was melted is
identified by ‘‘V”, as reported by Hallab and Jacobs [8]. The excellent
corrosion resistance of these stainless steels is due to their chromium
content (10.5–20 wt.%) which provides the formation of a protective
surface oxide layer. Nickel is an alloying element that stabilises the
formation of austenite in iron and also contributes to increasing the
corrosion resistance by forming protective oxide films on the surface of

the alloys [5]. However, it should be mentioned that nickel is highly
toxic to the human body [9, 10]. A great deal of research is being
focussed on developing nickel-free stainless steel by introducing large
amounts of nitrogen, which is an austenite stabilising element, instead
of nickel (which is also an austenite stabilising element). Comparing the
cytocompatibility of the thus produced nickel-free stainless-steel
containing Fe–Cr–Mo–N with 316 L stainless steel, the results indicate
that cell viability of nickel-free stainless steel is the best [11–13].
   The advantages associated with the use of stainless steels lie in that
they are relatively low priced, easily available, have excellent
fabrication properties, are biocompatible, and have great strength [11,
14]. The mechanical properties of stainless steel can be controlled in a
wide range and as such allows the fabricated products to possess
optimal ductility and strength for medical uses [15]. However, the
success of stainless steels makes these alloys widely accepted, but as
such, but they are not completely ‘‘stain-proof’’ taking into account that
the human body fluid is highly corrosive and the 316 L austenitic
stainless steels are not sufficiently corrosion resistant for long-term use
as an implant material. Hence, their applications are now confined to
temporary devices, such as internal fixation or traction devices. On the
other hand, inside of the human body, the skeletal bones suffer cyclic
loading in the course of patients walking. It is estimated that the step
number of a patient over 20 years is over 1 × 107 cycles [16]. This cyclic
loading may fracture the material below its ultimate tensile strength or
yield strength, according to investigations by Chen and Thouas [4].
Currently, the high-nitrogen stainless steel, Orthinox (ASTM 1586), is
the predominant stem material in the medical market of hip prosthesis
[4, 17].
     It is of paramount importance to know the biocompatibility of the
alloying elements used in the different stainless steels used in
orthopaedic implants and more specifically, the 316 L stainless steel
(ASTM F138), which is most commonly used in THA. The major alloying
elements in this stainless steel and variants are chromium, nickel,
molybdenum, and manganese, in addition to the matrix element, iron
[4]. Nevertheless, iron, chromium and nickel are the three dominant
elements with highlighted bioactivity related to the release of elements
as either soluble ions or insoluble particles [18].

Iron is a necessary element in almost all living organisms and is
present in all cells in the human body, fulfilling several vital functions
such as catalase and lipoxygenases, and oxidising food nutrients to
produce energy [19], as well as being an essential component of
haemoglobin that binds and carries oxygen to the tissues from the
lungs. Iron deficiency can produce anaemia and also too little iron can
interfere with the above-mentioned vital functions leading to, in some
cases, morbidity and death [20]. Although there is no report on the
adverse effects induced by iron ions released from stainless steel
implants [21], large amounts of iron released from these metallic
implants can cause excessive levels of iron in the blood, producing
highly active free radicals which could damage DNA, proteins, lipids,
and other cellular components. Humans experience iron toxicity above
20 mg/kg of body mass, and 60 mg/kg is considered a lethal dose [4,
22]. Chromium is an element mainly used as an alloying element in
steels where it contributes to hardness, tempering and resistance to
oxidation. Likewise, chromium is a mineral that humans require in
trace amounts, however its mechanisms of action in the body and the
amounts needed for optimal health are not well defined. As a trace
element, chromium is a co-factor in the regulation of sugar levels in
blood and deficiency of this may cause hyperglycaemia (elevated blood
sugar) and glucosuria (glucose in the urine). Hence, its concentrations
must be at safe levels in exposed individuals [1–3, 5, 7–13, 15–106]
inasmuch as elevated Cr levels have been reported to cause DNA and
chromosomal damage, and possibly hypersensitivity reactions [107].
However, to date there has been no significant epidemiological
evidence to link any of these changes with an increased incidence in
any reported disease. To establish what might be an acceptable level of
chromium, guidelines need to be established to standardise
measurements of ion concentration and bioavailability in this complex
subject. Lately, the metallic orthopaedic implants have generated health
concerns due to the toxic levels of Cr released by MoM bearing surface
[108–110]. The release of Cr nanoparticles from metallic orthopaedic
implant devices represents an internal exposure to metals that is not
dependent on absorption through barrier membranes and exemplifies
a still relatively unexplored field of toxicology according to Keegan et al.
[111]. On the other hand, it has been determined that these implants

release particulate metal debris in the form of corrosion particles, with
or without abrasion, which are primarily nanometre-sized [112]. Data
from the literature indicates a range of 5–100 mg/L of Cr present in
plasma and tissues from patients with MoM implants at revision
surgery [113]. Histologically, an inflammatory reaction often associated
with tissue necrosis/infarction is observed and is known as an adverse
reaction to metallic debris (ARMD) [114, 115]. There is a consensus
that this reaction is likely owing to a combination of both ion toxicity
and hypersensitivity reaction, which is particularly enhanced in some
patients for reasons still not well understood [108].
     It is well known that stainless steel commonly used in THA contains
chromium, nickel, manganese, molybdenum, and a low concentration of
carbon. Likewise, there is the general consensus that the nickel is
problematic due to its toxicity and its overall harmful effect on living
organisms. Therefore, in order to solve this problem, nickel-free
stainless steels were developed, resulting in the introduction of steels
with increased nitrogen [116]. However, corrosion and the consequent
release of metal ions into periprosthetic tissue are inevitable when
metallic replacements are implanted even though, metabolically, metal
ions are essential but can be cytotoxic, genotoxic, carcinogenic, or
allergenic in high concentrations [117, 118]. Nonetheless, it is clear that
patients receiving MoM in THA have increased concentrations of metal
ions in their blood and urine according to a report by MacDonald et al.
[117], hence there is a necessity to clearly define the boundary between
normal and toxic concentrations [116]. On the other hand, from the
different ions released from metallic replacements, nickel is the one
preferentially released from these replacements [119]. So far, some
studies have been unable to provide clear boundaries for
concentrations of different metallic ions in patients with THA and
therefore, further research is needed to enable the early diagnosis of a
metal allergy in these patients. It seems that the metal sensitivity can
play a role in causing problems with implants. Having said that, patch
testing can discern the dilemma whether or not the patient is allergic to
the exposure of nickel, but of course this does not establish a definite
cause and effect relationship between the problem with an implant and
a nickel allergy. However, the absence of a positive patch test will be of
more value in ruling out such a relationship [120].

4.2 Cobalt Based Alloys
In comparison to stainless steel, cobalt-based alloys have a longer
lifespan and are less likely to experience fatigue fracture [121]. Cobalt-
based alloys were first used in medical implants in the 1930s with the
first adaption of a cobalt-based alloy in biomedical implantation being
reported in 1936 for THA [122]. Approximately 10 years later, its
medical applications in orthopaedics were significantly expanded,
reporting notable successes [4, 123]. Based on the composition,
biomedical Co-based alloys are typically categorised into two groups as
follows: (i) first group Co-Cr–Mo alloy, which contains 27–30% Cr and
5–7% Mo and (ii) second group Co–Ni-Cr–Mo whose composition
includes Ni (33–37%), Cr (19–21%) and Mo (9–11%). The corrosion
resistance of these CoCr alloys is more than an order of magnitude
greater than that of stainless steels, and they possess excellent
mechanical properties [124]. Moreover, a number of compositions have
been developed, identified as F75-98 (Co–28Cr–6Mo), F562-95 (Co–
35Ni–20Cr–10Mo), and F961-96 (Co–35Ni–20Cr–10Mo) amongst
others, which are used as permanent implants [5, 125] resulting in
orthopaedic replacements which are highly corrosion resistant, even in
chloride-rich environments.
   Despite the corrosion resistance provided by both cobalt and
chromium, one of the major issues of this alloy is its biocorrosion [14,
126]. MoM implants tend to create between 1012–1014 nanoparticles of
cobalt–chromium (Co–Cr) alloy per year, in the size range of 20–60 nm,
where the presence of these nanoparticles near the implant site has an
antibacterial characteristic preventing formation of biofilms. On the
other hand, in isolation, the heavy metals contained within the wear
debris (cobalt and nickel) have been clearly shown to retard the growth
of bacteria, particularly nickel. Studies have shown that increased levels
of cobalt and chromium in the serum can also be seriously related to
implant loosening [127, 128]. Hence, inflammatory responses are
observed near the implant showing tissue necrosis, ulceration, and
allergic reactions [14, 129, 130]. It is well known that nickel is also
often employed as an alloying element in the Co based alloys inasmuch
as it increases the stacking fault energy of the alloy, stabilising the γ
phase rather than the ε phase, thereby achieving a higher ductility

[131]. However, knowing the high toxicity of nickel, Ni-free cobalt alloys
are being developed for biomedical applications. In another scenario,
the lack of integration of the Co–Cr alloy into the bone also leads to
implant failure so it becomes necessary to modify its surface, including
covalent protein grafting and self-assembled monolayers of certain
chemicals, to mention a few. Similar to nickel, cobalt toxicity has been
reported in some patients with MoM hip replacements after 4–5 years
of implantation [132], with a Co content around 5–300 mg/L in plasma
and tissue according to literature data [113]. As stated by Tower’s
investigations [133], patients with a cobalt implant are at risk for cobalt
poisoning and might present with cardiac or some other neurological
symptoms. Although imperfect [4], cobalt alloys are still regarded as a
favourite metallic implant material in joint bearing applications.
Conversely, the high costs involved in manufacturing have put Co-based
alloys at another disadvantage when it comes to the medical market.

4.3 Titanium and Its Alloys
Amongst the different metallic alloys available for orthopaedic
applications, the selection of titanium-based materials for implantation
is due to their outstanding characteristics such as high strength, low
density (high specific strength), high immunity to corrosion, enhanced
biocompatibility, complete inertness to body environment, as well as
the high capacity to join with bone and other tissues [60, 134].
Titanium for orthopaedic implants fabrication dates back to the late
1930s, and it was found that titanium was well tolerated in cat femurs,
like other implant materials such as stainless steel and vitallium (a Co-
Cr–Mo alloy). Commercially pure Ti and Ti-6Al-4 V ELI (Ti64, Extra Low
interstitial) are the most commonly used titanium materials for implant
applications; however, commercially pure hcp titanium CPTi is used,
particularly for dental implants. Nonetheless, the main disadvantage of
CPTi, and to some extent also of Ti-6Al-4 V compared to F75 cobalt-
based alloys, is that it is relatively soft. Considering that the Ti64 alloy
was originally developed for aerospace applications, its high corrosion
resistance and excellent biocompatibility allowed its use in the
biomedical industry [135]. The absence of chromium, cobalt or nickel
in the titanium alloys causes the alloy to have a lower resistance

strength [116, 136], but conversely, it is physiologically inert and highly
adherent to newly formed bone [137, 138].
   Despite all these advantages, the long-term performance of these
alloys has raised some concerns due mainly to the release of metals like
aluminium and vanadium, from Ti64 alloys, that have been shown to be
associated with health problems such as Alzheimer’s disease (currently
this finding is controversial), neuropathy, and osteomalacia [14, 139,
140] On the other hand, it is important to note that vanadium alone is
toxic in both elemental and oxide states at the surface of the
orthopaedic replacement [141]. In light of the aforementioned, V-free
Ti alloys such as Ti-6Al-7Nb and Ti-5Al-2.5Fe have been developed
parallel to obtaining aluminium free alloys, where V-and Al-free Ti
alloys such as Ti-Zr and Ti-Sn alloys have been investigated and
developed [14, 142–144]. One of the big problems with the use of
titanium alloys is its severe wear when it comes in contact with other
metal surfaces owing to a high coefficient of friction, thus causing
inflammation of the surrounding tissues leading to the inevitable
loosening of the implants [145]. Therefore, thermomechanical
processing of these alloys is required to increase wear resistance [146,
147]. Unlike the toxicity of alloying elements such as Ni, Co or Cr, it has
been well reported that titanium is totally inert to the body
environment [15, 124, 148] and in the event of an excess of titanium in
a living body, excretion would take place without any absorption or
digestion [149]. This inertness seems to make Ti and Ti-alloys the
perfect material for orthopaedic implants. Nevertheless, effects such as
osteomalacia, allergic reaction, and peripheral neuropathy have been
found in some Ti-alloy implanted bodies, likely due to the release of
aluminium and vanadium from the alloy, according to reports by Geetha
et al. [134], Manivasagam et al. [150] and Niinomi [151]. Considering
that commercially pure titanium CP Ti and its alloys are nowadays
being extensively employed for their excellent mechanical properties in
orthopaedic replacements, attempts at replacing Al and V (toxic
elements) by relatively safer elements such as Mo, Ta, Nb and Zr have
been carried out [60, 135] leading to a new V-free α + β-type Ti-based
alloy, i.e., Ti-6Al-7Nb with good mechanical and metallurgical behaviour
in comparison to those of Ti-6Al-4 V. Nevertheless, several studies, for
example Evans [152] and Rho et al. [153] have shown that the elastic

modulus of α-type and some α + β-type Ti-based alloys is much higher
than that of human bone which could cause a stress shielding effect
[154, 155]. In light of this and to alleviate the stress shielding effect, low
cost β-Ti-based alloys with low modulus and composed of low cost
elements such as Fe, Cr, Mn and Sn, have been proposed to reduce the
consumption of high cost elements such as Nb, Ta and Zr. Examples of
them are Ti-15Mo, Ti-13Nb-13Zr, Ti-12Mo-6Zr-2Fe, Ti-35Nb-5Ta-7Zr,
and Ti-29Nb-13Ta-4.6Zr [154, 156, 157]. It is very important to stress
that the lowest elastic modulus reported so far in bulk Ti-based alloys
developed for biomedical applications is 40 GPa for Ti-35Nb-4Sn alloy
[158]. Regrettably, this value is still greater than that of cortical bone
(10–30 GPa) and so far, it is very difficult to lower the elastic modulus
of bulk Ti-based alloys below 40 GPa [154].
   Within the characteristics researchers have been pursuing is the
development of Ti-based alloys with low elastic modulus and therefore,
porous materials seem to be a great alternative to achieve this goal,
taking into consideration that these type of materials can provide
better biological fixation by promoting bone tissue ingrowth into the
pores of the implants so allowing homogeneous stress transfer
between bones and implants [171, 172], as well as a good combination
of mechanical strength with low elastic modulus. In fact, porous Ti-
based alloys can overcome the mechanical weakness present in the
porous ceramics and polymeric materials as well as eliminating the
problems of biomechanical mismatch of elastic modulus [154]. In spite
of the advantages of porous materials, certain limitations continue to
exist related with the fabrication processes. Hence, the focus remains
on the β-type Ti-based alloys, newly developed for biomedical
applications, whose composition and elastic modulus, together with an
indication of the processing methods employed, are shown in Table 4.1

of why Ti and Ti-alloys are regarded as the most promising metallic
biomaterial to date.

4.4 Tantalum and Its Alloys
Tantalum (Ta) is a hard and ductile transition metal, chemically very
resistant to corrosion (due to the stable, native, Ta2O5 protective film
formed on the surface), especially to acids, and it is a good conductor of
heat and electricity [173]. It is rather rare in nature and is found in the
mineral tantalite and is completely immune to body fluids. It is also a
non-irritating metal which is intended for an increased use in the bone-
implant interface of cementless implants [174] due to its
biocompatibility and excellent osseointegration properties. At the
present time, with the increasing number of young, active people
undergoing THA, it is necessary to find an alternative material with
adequate biological and mechanical properties [14]. However,
tantalum’s high cost and high density makes the manufacture of large

implants difficult. Moreover, the high melting temperature (>3000 °C)
of this metal makes it difficult for processing using traditional alloying
methods leading to the use of powder metallurgical routes for its
shaping [1]. In other words, the applications of tantalum in biomedical
devices have been severely limited by processing challenges rather than
biological performances [175]. It is well known that titanium alloy
prostheses have demonstrated a high resistance to corrosion, but under
sliding and friction with other materials, titanium suffers from large
erosion producing a lot of released particles and provoking a premature
prosthesis failure. In this situation, orthopaedic prostheses made of
porous tantalum have demonstrated very good performances, a crucial
parameter to extend the life service of the replacement [176]. Currently,
porous tantalum is available for use in several orthopaedic applications,
mainly THA and TKA.
   An excellent feature of porous tantalum is its modulus of elasticity
(approximately 3 GPa) which is very similar to that of subchondral
bone (2 GPa) which in turn facilitates the growth of new bone over the
prosthesis producing a better stress distribution and diminishing the
bone resorption [182, 183]. Likewise, it is important to note that
tantalum does not elicit the cytotoxicity levels associated with some
other metals, such as nickel, cobalt, and chromium [184]. On the other
hand, and considering that the porosity is important in an implant
inasmuch as the bone is living tissue that grows into your implant,
incorporating it into your body, the tantalum-based material that is
more commonly used in human implants is commercially known
Trabecular metal® and is characterised by its 75–80% of porosity in
comparison to only 35–50% of porosity in other materials used for
orthopaedics [185–187]. Trabecular metal® performs as a wonderful
structure for the growth of new bone [176]. Therefore, important
factors such as porosity, pore size and interconnectivity must be
considered for the design and optimisation of porous tantalum
prostheses. The two main methods to fabricate them are (i) via
chemical vapour infiltration (CVI) and (ii) via a Laser Multi-layer
Cladding Engineered (LMCE) through cladding layer by layer. Porous
trabecular metal (TM) shows an open-cell structure (Fig. 4.1a)
comprised of repeating dodecahedrons with a microstructural
appearance similar to cancellous bone (Fig. 4.1b) [188].

Fig. 4.1 Microstructure of the trabecular metal (TM) (a), and cancellous bone (b) [188]
   This cancellous-like structure, interconnected porosity and
excellent bone in-growth potential are an important and unique
combination of attributes that contribute to the osteoconductive
properties of Trabecular Metal Technology [185, 189]. In short,
depending on the required application, tantalum implants can be
available in bulk form (usually porous) and in coating form, generally as
tantalum oxides. However, in spite of its excellent properties in vitro
and in vivo in the form of porous implants, the high cost of
manufacturing and the impossibility of producing modular implants
have limited the acceptance of tantalum [190]. Clinical studies in
patients have shown that Trabecular Metal technology provides several
unique advantages over other joint replacement materials [191].

4.5 Niobium and Its Alloys
Recently, niobium alloys are being proposed for biomedical
applications and Nb-2Zr, which shows excellent corrosion resistance,
fatigue strength, and crack propagation in simulated body fluids [14,
192], has been introduced. While niobium has little known biological
roles in humans, some niobium-containing compounds are toxic,
including niobates and niobium chloride, two chemicals that are water
soluble [4, 193]. According to Chen and Thouas [4] and Downs et al.
[193], one study found niobium to be one of the more toxic metal ions,

along with cobalt, tested for their ability to induce DNA damage and
cause immune cell death [194]. Therefore, this element should be
treated with care, especially when several alloying elements are used.
In spite of the mentioned problems, niobium (Nb) has been recently
studied as a possible implant candidate in its pure form due to its
attractive properties [195]. Different investigations related to the
biological response of the cells in contact with Nb are originated from
the evaluation of TiNbx alloys [196], in which Nb had been introduced
as a substitute for Al or V (metallic elements associated with health
problems) [197–199] and in all cases, it was demonstrated that the
short and long-term biocompatibility of Nb was excellent, being a good
alloying substitute providing mechanical strength to the Ti alloys as
well as being a biocompatible element. On the other hand, studies by
Eisenbarth et al. [141] showed that in tested samples of pure crystalline
Nb (cp-Nb), the cell proliferation, the mitochondrial activity, and the
cell volume were similar and superior to those of Ti and stainless steel
samples, respectively.
   Likewise, investigations have shown the potential use of porous
titanium–niobium alloys in orthopaedic implants fabricated by means
of powder metallurgy (PM) technology for small parts with a
complicated shape [200, 201], and to obtain porous titanium–niobium
alloys with different porosities and a mechanical strength similar to
cortical bone. Figure 4.2 illustrates a Ti-25Nb alloy material composed
by a porous structure with a rough surface after high-temperature
sintering in a vacuum. The measured diameter of pores was about 200–
50 µm (Fig. 4.2a–d) with a three-dimensional connectivity between
them. The pores of the Ti-25Nb alloy with 70% porosity showed a
honeycomb structure with fractures and connectivity. It is important to
note that irregular pore shapes, inappropriate pore size,
inhomogeneous pore distribution, and inhomogeneous elemental
distribution could be factors that occur when the PM processing
technique is used, however, for clinical biological materials and
especially alloys, characteristics such as chemical composition,
roughness, the internal pore size, and porosity are factors important to
take into account [202] to obtain good biocompatibility, regardless of
the percentage of porosity, in accordance with the above mentioned for
the porous tantalum-based material (Trabecular metal®).

4.6 Mg Alloys
Magnesium alloys fall into the third category of implant biomaterials
and their potential application for orthopaedic implants is based in
benefits such as (i) benign macro-element in the body [203] showing
good resorbability and high biocompatibility [204], (ii) similar density
and Young’s modulus similar to that of bone, and (iii) controllable
corrosion rates (and thus resorbability) in physiological media [4].
Magnesium is a light metal with a density of 1.74 g/cm3 and is 1.6–4.5
times lighter than aluminium and, respectively, steel [205]. Magnesium

alloys commercially available today include WE43 [Mg-Y-RE (rare
earth)-Zr system], AZ91 (Mg–Al–Zn alloy system), AZ 31 (Mg–Al–Zn–
Mn alloy system) and LAE442 (Mg–Li–Al–RE–Mn alloy system) [14,
206–208]. Taking into account that magnesium is the fourth most
abundant element in the human body, magnesium alloy properties
mainly depend on the processing techniques where the primary
processing of biodegradable Mg alloys are classified as either solid state
or liquid state techniques [209]. Powder metallurgy is a solid state
synthesis technique involving blending the metal powders for the
desired composition, then pressing and sintering the material, and
casting is an economic liquid state technique by super heating the
material above 750 °C in an inert gas atmosphere to protect from
oxidation, followed by transferring the metal to the mould and allowing
it to solidify [209]. Nevertheless, regardless of the manufacturing
method of the magnesium alloys to be used as an effective
biodegradable implant, it is very important to control their corrosion
behaviour in the body fluid environment [210, 211]. Knowing that
there are three major groups of Mg alloys (the first group consists of
pure Mg; the second group consists of aluminium (Al) containing alloys
and rare earth elements (RE), and the final group consists of the Al free
alloys such as Mg-Ca, WE, MZ and WZ), the alloying elements such as Al,
Ca, Li, Mn, Y, Zn, Zr and RE in Mg alloys improve the physical and
mechanical properties of these alloys, refining the grain structure,
improving the corrosion resistance, form inter-metallic phases that can
enhance the strength, and assist in the manufacture and shaping of Mg
alloys [210, 212]. However, there is a definite requirement to carefully
select alloying elements that are non-toxic to the human body, such as
Ca [213] and Zr [214], which improve the corrosion resistance of the
Mg alloy and reduce the degradation rate suggesting the Mg metal alloy
as a viable implant material [215]. Despite a substantial number of
research reports supporting the use of magnesium alloys as potential
orthopaedic biodegradable implants, studies are still needed to
adequately assess this potential metal with special properties [205],
emphasising that it is difficult to choose the best alloy inasmuch as
more in vitro and in vivo experiments and clinical investigation is
required [216].

Although the studies on the magnesium based materials have been
successfully conducted on patented/protected compositions and
composites (see Table 4.3), the choice of these alloys as biomaterials is
still limited for materials selection, and undoubtedly its portfolio needs
significant enhancement to scale from smaller implants (pins, clips and
screws) to larger implants (such as plates), and as scaffolds [217]. For
this reason, the key challenge is to control the degradation rate at
different levels, considering the function of the implant as well as its
required lifetime in the human body. Furthermore, it is of paramount
importance for the material scientists that the inherent composition of
the implant does not release ions or corrosion products that can create
local or systemic toxicity [210, 212, 213, 218–225] inasmuch as several
options exist for alloying elements to obtain Mg-based implants.

The etiology for implant failure is becoming increasingly important. Available literatures concerning the
relationship between metal allergy and implant failure is controversial and it is difficult to determine
whether sensitization is a cause or a consequence of implant failure. As consequence of the
ineffectiveness of preoperative patch testing with the purpose to predict adverse outcomes, as well as
the high cost of implementing such patch testing as standard procedure, most orthopedists and
dermatologists agree that an alternative prosthesis should only be considered for patients with a
history of allergy to a metal in the standard implant. Hence, collaboration between orthopedists and
dermatologists when evaluating joint replacement patients with a presentation suggestive of allergy is
necessary.
  THA has been a major and standard treatment of disabilities of the hip achieving predictably
excellent clinical results [1] and relatively low peri-operative morbidity [2]. Considering an increased
demand for joint replacement in younger, more active patients requiring increased implant longevity,
the number of TKA and THA has been projected to increase dramatically up until 2030 [3]. It is very
important to remember that when introducing an implant into the human body, organism will treat it as
an alien body and different reactions can be expected [4] where cutaneous and systemic
hypersensitivity reactions to implanted metallic orthopaedic prosthesis are not so rare [5–9]. It is well
known that the chemical compounds present in metallic implants are, as a rule, well accepted by the
body, although they may have toxic, carcinogen effects or cause allergies [8]. Undoubtedly, the different
reactions of the body to implants depend on general body factors such as the appearance of current
inside the implant, the corrosion process, and friction.
  On the other hand, the implant surface is subjected to reaction from the tissue as well as body
liquids during the process of oxidation, causing the penetration into the tissue of toxic ions like
vanadium, nickel and chromium, and then, an infection can be originated by microorganisms which are
stuck to the surface of the implant [8, 9]. Likewise, the release of nanoparticles and metal ions owing to
implant corrosion is a major concern following THA and TKA, and metal debris derived from
orthopaedic implants can be found in both synovial fluid and peri-prosthetic tissues, circulating
through the lymphatic and vascular systems [2]. In this context, and despite the high success rate of
THA and TKA [2, 10, 11], about 10–20% of arthroplasties annually are revised due to implant failure
[12] with instability and infection being the most common causes of failure [13, 14]. Nevertheless, in
recent decades, attention has been drawn to metal hypersensitivity (MHS) as another possible cause of

failure [15]. MHS is a rare condition where the body develops an immunological reaction to the metallic
portion of THA or TKA implants [16].
    Strictly speaking, the prevalence of MHS is about 10–15% [17–20] with nickel being the most
common allergy-inducing metal (19.7–24.4%), followed by cobalt (2–8.8%) and chromium (2.4–5.9%)
[21]. In extreme cases, a cross-hypersensitivity reaction for all three metals [22] has been observed
where multiple factors can promote MHS and, for example, female patients are more sensitive to nickel
[23] whereas male patients to chromate [24]. Moreover, there are variations related with the status of
the implant such as well-functioning implants and poorly functioning implants or loosening of the
prosthesis [17, 18, 20]. Some studies have disclosed that this phenomenon may be attributed to the fact
that the MHS reaction is elicited by continuous contact with metal ions, thus inducing an allergic
reaction [25]. In regard of this, nowadays the modern implants are all coated with plasma spray to limit
metal ion exposure [18, 26] but even such a coating has a great disadvantage, providing a rough surface
which may increase the available area for ion release [17].
   Considering the complexity of MHS, several study groups have focussed on the investigation of the
cause-and-effect relationship between MHS reactions and implant failure in orthopaedic and trauma
surgery [1]. It is found that MHS may present a variety of symptoms as follows: (i) pain, (ii) joint
effusion, (iii) delayed wound/bone healing, (iv) persistent secretion, (v) allergic dermatitis (localised or
systemic), and (vi) implant instability and failure, amongst others. Nevertheless, the underlying
mechanisms still remain to be fully elucidated and therefore, the way that MHS is presented is
inconsistent and as a consequence of the diagnostic difficulties, the reported statistics may be not
realistic. Hence, the potential clinical implications for the patient after implantation of a foreign body is
seriously considered as an important topic for the surgical community [1, 27]. After these
implantations, the allergic complications imply cutaneous changes such as eczema, urticarial, and
impaired wound healing, but also extracutaneous reactions such as swelling, effusions, pain, and even
loosening [2, 19, 25–32]. It is noteworthy that the MHS is frequently a diagnosis of exclusion and it is
only considered after infection, implant malposition, instability, and fractures have been ruled out [33].
   Since MHS is a controversial issue, several research groups are working on the topic “implant
allergy” because there are somewhat differing opinions on the diagnostic approaches [28, 34–37]. After
several studies (for example Thyssen et al. [27] and Granchi et al. [20]) a consensus could be that the
two most common methods of testing for MHS are (in vivo) skin patch testing and (in vitro) the
lymphocyte transformation test (LTT). In theory and according to the report by Thomas et al. [38], the
testing could be done in patients undergoing their first implantation or alternatively, in patients with
metallic implant failure. Because of the challenge involved in the diagnosis of MHS, various diagnostic
algorithms and tests have been proposed but presently there is no generally established guidelines [1].
Although the skin patch testing is yet considered to be an excellent initial test for evaluating potential
allergens [39] and can present for accurately predicting MHS, it has been recommended that patients
who have reported a history of metal allergy, for example, contact with jewellery or clothing
accessories, undergo preoperative screening via skin patch testing [1, 2, 39]. One positive result of this
test leads to the use of a component made of hypoallergenic materials, such as titanium, zirconium, or
ceramics [1, 40]. These alternatives could include surface modifications of conventional implants, which
has been studied in depth by Bader et al. [41]. Surface modifications such as oxygen diffusion hardening
(ODH), nitrogen-ion implanted mechanisms, diamond-like-carbon (DLC) coating, as well as PVD
coatings, are alternatives available for titanium and cobalt-chromium alloys, and are manufactured by
various companies worldwide [1]. However, compared to conventional orthopaedic implants, such
alternatives present disadvantages such as higher costs, and increased surgical time in the beginning
owing to the need of becoming familiar with a new implant. On the other hand, cracking, gouging and
delamination of coatings/modified surfaces, potentially result in wear and implant failure [42].
   Despite the aforementioned, an ideal diagnostic of MHS in orthopaedic and trauma surgery remains
controversial and therefore, the tests for implant-related hypersensitivity must be performed and
interpreted by experienced teams. As reported Lohmann et al. [1] the management of patients with
(suspected) implant-related hypersensitivity remains greater challenge in orthopaedic and trauma
surgery. Table 5.1 illustrates details of individual case studies for patients with metal hypersensitivity
and managed with a variety of approaches. The outcomes disclosed that patients were treated with

surgical revision utilising hypoallergenic prostheses such as titanium based implants, zirconium-nickel
coated implants, zirconium-ceramic alloy implants, as well as cobalt and ceramic alloy coated implants
and one ceramic implant [43–51]. In spite of that both TKA and THA patients may present joint pain
and swelling, but the cutaneous reaction is not common among THA patients, as reported by Willert et
al. [52] and Zeng and Feng [53]. Additional to this, radiographic studies revealed osteolytic lesions in
the proximity of the hip or knee implant as a result of the inflammatory response which in turn can
result in aseptic loosening of the metallic implant [10, 15]. It is noteworthy that in some cases, the
allergic phenomenon resulted in the necessity of removing the implant [4, 54, 55] due to severe allergic
skin inflammation, urticaria, and inflation of the blood vessels [55]. Additionally, some rash changes
may be located in the vicinity of an implant or even, appear in different places (blood eczema), as well
as complications such as metallosis (metallic colouring of surrounding tissues) and fibrosis around the
implant, and tissue necrosis. Although the incidence of adverse local tissue reactions is relatively low
(5.3% of THA complications) but potentially challenging complication after THA [56], it is generally
associated with MoM prosthetic devices, but has also been described in non-metallic prostheses [57–
59] and can lead to serious complications affecting the nervous system, skin and other organs. The
diagnosis of this complication is made at joint aspiration only [60], when dense black fluid is obtained,
so fluid analysis is not essential but the surgical revision with replacement of the prosthesis
components is needed. However, the complete removal of all metal debris is very difficult and may
result in extensive tissue damage [60]. On the other hand, surgeons sometimes encounter metallic
debris embedded in periarticular soft tissues or implants during revision surgery in a well-functioning,
well-fixed metal-on-polyethylene THA [60]. This condition leads to friction between the head and
acetabular components when either of these two components is made of a metal, and metal wear
particles will be generated in addition to polyethylene (PE) wear particles, and thus, ‘metallosis’
develops [61–64]. For all metallosis cases, at revision, surgeons may see black fluid filling the effective
joint space as well as greyish periprosthetic tissues, suggestive of metallosis, as can be seen in Fig. 5.1
[61]. The removal of the metallic debris embedded in tissues is very difficult and often resembles tar. It
is argued that in non-cemented implants, the metallosis can cause its dislocation as the healthy tissue
that would normally hold the implant in place is weakened or destroyed [60, 65].

    Certainly, the true causes of allergy to metals are nowadays not fully known and no diagnostic
method exists. Indeed, on one hand, some patients who underwent metal implantation developed a
tolerance to metals, and on the other some of them experienced dermatologic and/or orthopaedic
complications [66]. Undoubtedly, improvements in design and tribology have reduced the incidence in
modern components and a follow-up could prevent development of metallosis with catastrophic
consequences like gross implant loosening leading to a more complex revision [60]. In this context,
novel trials are needed to closely examine the patients with metallic allergies to provide sufficient
results for an evidence-based approach [5].
