Total hip replacement surgery is among the most successful procedures
performed by orthopedic surgeons providing both immediate and long-
term relief to persons suffering severe issues such as hip arthritis, hip
osteonecrosis, or other complex hip problems. Ceramic hip implants
are among the latest types of prostheses developed for hip replacement
taking advantage of its greater resistance to damage and smooth
movement of the joint. They are considered to be an improvement over
traditional metal-and-plastic implants in which the deterioration of
plastic can lead to the gradual build-ups of debris around the joint
leading to inflammation and the development of benign cysts known as
pseudotumors. On the other side, ceramic devices appear to cause far
less (if any) inflammation pseudotumors. Advanced bioceramics are

expected to have increasing use in orthopaedics taking into account
their unique combination and range of properties including strength
and toughness, hardness and wear resistance, biocompatibility,
bacteriostasis, and osseointegration.
   The generation of low concentrations of wear particles is the main
requirement for a material used as a bearing surface in joint
arthroplasty. For a long time THA was affected by wear debris which
induces osteolysis, as well as loss of fixation [1, 2]. In the light of the
recent problems with metal-on-metal bearing couplings and according
to Oosthuizen and Snyckers [3], it is certainly now time to question the
efficacy and safety of every new implant that is nowadays introduced
into the arthroplasty market. Considering this, at present, there are
different bearing surface combinations for use in the clinic such as
highly cross-linked polyethylene with metal or ceramic heads [4, 5],
MoM [6] resurfacing only as a niche product, otherwise MoM was
banned, and CoC [7]. Now, exposure to high concentrations of metal
ions for longer periods [8, 9] in younger and more active patients, or
women of reproductive age, can be of particular concern. Thus, CoC
couplings have excellent biocompatibility and higher wear and scratch
resistance (extremely important in off-normal conditions) than other
bearing surfaces [10, 11]. As a bearing surface in THA, ceramics have
been used for more than 40 years. Their excellent properties such as
hardness and highlighted wettability make them attractive for this
application. However, low fracture toughness and linear elastic
behaviour demonstrated by ceramics make them prone to breakage
under stress. Nevertheless, with the alumina matrix composite and
proper insert geometry, ceramic fracture is not an issue anymore
Improvements in the processing of ceramics, as well as advances in
engineering of head-neck articulations and liner design have produced
a decrease in the incidence of ceramic fracture and dislocation [12].
Dislocation is mostly head diameter related. Large diameters lead to a
lower risk for recurrent dislocations. ZTA also allows for thinner liners
such that a larger head can be implanted on the same acetabulum. In
order to replace CoCr surfaces in THA and TKA, ceramic materials were
introduced by Boutin in 1970 to improve the lower-friction surface, as
well as to obtain a smoother surface in comparison with CoCr, and thus
minimise PE wear. Undoubtedly, less wear is in evidence when ceramic

surfaces are used in THA [13, 14] and TKA [15] replacement surgery,
instead of CoCr [16], and these favourable qualities are very desirable
for implants in high-demand patients, such as the aforementioned
young or more active patients [1, 10, 17]. It is well known that both the
science and application of biomaterials in orthopaedic implants has had
an explosive growth during the past 50 years [18] with THA being the
most successful operation of the 20th century [19], and the ceramic
materials have been integral to this evolution. In fact, the orthopaedists
welcomed the use of these materials because of their favourable
properties such as biocompatibility, strength, hardness, wear, and
corrosion resistance [18]. During this period, alumina, hydroxyapatite,
zirconia, ceramic-coated metals and ZTA proliferated. An elegant in-
depth study concerning most of these ceramic biomaterials is collected
in the published work by Piconi et al. [20]. Currently, ceramics and
some ceramic coated devices have been incorporated into various
prostheses, almost from inception, either for osseous-fixation or
articulation devices. Amongst these, Al2O3, ZrO2, ZTA, alumina-
toughened zirconia (ATZ), hydroxyapatite (HAp) and bioactive ceramics
are the commonly selected ceramic materials for applications in
orthopaedics replacement [18].

6.1 Bioactive Ceramics
The bioactivity of a material is defined as its ability to bond biologically
to bone and they are employed as coatings to enhance the fixation of a
device or as bone-graft substitutes because of their osteoconductive
properties [21]. Calcium phosphate, glass, glass–ceramic, and
composites are included within this category and have the capability to
interact with the biological environment with the aim to improve the
host response, as well as bind the injured tissue. Nevertheless, these
materials can undergo progressive degradation while the new tissue
regenerates [22, 23]. An important characteristic of these bioactive
ceramics is related to the time-dependent kinetic modification of the
surface which occurs upon implantation [24–26]. A biologically active
hydroxycarbonate apatite (HCA) layer is thus formed on the surface,
which in turn provides the bonding interface with tissues where this
layer is equivalent chemically, and structurally, to the mineral phase in

bone [24]. Nowadays, some bioactive ceramics have already been used
with the purpose to repair bone defects, achieving tight fixation as a
consequence of direct bonding to living bone. A glass in the Na2O–CaO–
SiO2–P2O5 system was the first bioactive ceramic developed [24, 27]
and known as Bioglass. Since the discovery of this Bioglass, various
types of bioactive ceramics have been developed, such as sintered
hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2 [28, 29], glass–ceramic Ceravital [30],
and glass–ceramic (apatite/wollastonite) A–W [31, 32], to name a few.
Nevertheless, these bioactive ceramics have lower fracture toughness
and a Young’s modulus higher than cortical bone leading to limited
applications in the replacement of bony parts under low loads, and
mainly as bone fillers [33]. In reason of the above mentioned, the
development of alternative bioactive materials that not only show
bioactivity, but also a wide spectrum of mechanical and biological
properties similar to living bone that provides the opportunity of using
them as substitutes in load bearing positions, is needed [33, 34]. In
spite of different issues of some bioactive ceramics, the successful
experimental evidence in vitro and in vivo generated by 45S5 Bioglass
(a silicate network which incorporates sodium, calcium and
phosphorus with a composition of 45% SiO2, 24.5% Na2O, 24.5% CaO
and 6% P2O5), has allowed it to reach the governmental regulatory
approval for its clinical use [34, 35] in applications for the treatment of
periodontal diseases, and for middle ear surgery as well as for
orthopaedic applications under the commercial name NovaBone® [36–
39]. As an example, Table 6.1 illustrates some mechanical properties of
human cancellous and cortical bone in comparison to commonly used
dense bioactive glass 45S5 Bioglass® [40], where it can be seen that the
compressive strength of these bioactive glasses is >1.5 times higher
than the highest strength reported for trabecular bone (0.1–16 MPa).
Likewise, the observed variations in compressive strength values could

characterised by sample geometry, size, loading speed and so on.
Similarly, a wide range of values reported for the compressive modulus

emphasising that these bioactive ceramics are not being used and
cannot be used in joint replacement inasmuch as it will not last a single

6.2 Alumina Ceramics
As mentioned above, THA is the most successful procedure used to
treat end-stage degenerative conditions of the hip [53–55]. In spite of
substantial improvements in prosthetic designs and surgical
techniques, THA in young and active patients remains poorer than that
in their older counterparts [56–58]. The generation of wear debris,
which may lead to periprosthetic osteolysis, is one of the material-
related issues in THA [59]. The conventional PE is almost no longer
used in hips. With this background and with the aim of reducing wear,

limiting osteolysis progression, and extending implant longevity in
young and active patients, bearing surfaces made of alumina ceramic
were introduced in 1971 [60]. During the last 45 years, alumina
ceramics have continuously improved, resulting in a pure material that
fulfils the clinical requirements [61]. The type used is a polycrystalline
α-Al2O3, often referred to simply as Al2O3, consisting of a single
crystalline phase (the α–phase corundum), made up of a large number
of small grains, typically with a size less than a few micrometres [62].
MgO (Magnesia) amounts (~0.25 wt.%) as a sintering aid to control the
grain size are commonly added in order to promote nearly theoretical
density. A dense fine-grained alumina could possess an exceptional
hardness and wear resistance. Alumina has shown to decrease the
polyethylene wear and can be used in hard-on-hard configurations,
consequently eliminating PE from THA articulations entirely [63–65].
Alumina is a chemically inert ceramic with very good biocompatibility
and extensive clinical experience [55]. Alumina implants used in
orthopaedic surgery are subject to quality standards according to the
ISO/DIS 6474-1 (updated in 2016) [66]. It is well known that CoC
exhibits remarkable mechanical properties but perhaps the most
important one is its low friction coefficient and excellent wear
resistance, with a wear rate 4000 times lower than that of MoP [55].
   However, early clinical performances of alumina-on-alumina THAs
ended up with very disappointing results owing to a high rate of
ceramic fractures, and loss of fixation of the socket where this was an
early design issue (screw cup), not material related. High fracture rates
of alumina femoral heads, from 6.9 to 13.4%, were cited during 1970
and 1976 according to reports by Boutin et al. [67], Griss and Heimke
[68] and Knahr et al. [69]. Nonetheless, a fracture rate as low as 0.4%
was also observed [70–72]. These variations are the result of
technological evolution over the years, from low purity raw material to
highly pure synthetic raw materials, from, direct sintering to hot
isostatic pressing (HIP) etc. [67–69]. As a consequence of the
technological evolution, low fracture rates are reported from medical-
grade alumina [70–74]. Figure 6.1 shows scanning electron
micrographs (SEM) of sintered industrial alumina (Fig. 6.1a) and
medical-grade alumina (Fig. 6.1b) where the differences in grain size
are evident, and undoubtedly the mechanical properties can also differ

from one material to another. Judging by the micrographs of Fig. 6.1, the
microstructure developed for industrial alumina applications is very
poor (Fig. 6.1a) characterised by insufficient purity, low density and
coarse grain size compared with alumina used for the manufacture of
hip prostheses, Fig. 6.1b.

   An important aspect to consider in the development of medical-
grade alumina is its impurities content. Glassy phases are commonly
found at the grain boundaries of some ceramic materials as a result of
these impurities contained in the raw materials. These tend to degrade
in the body and cause, amongst other things, the material to age, i.e. to
lose its mechanical strength [75–77]. Nowadays, the efforts made to
increase the purity of the alumina is reflected in the production of the
so called 3rd generation alumina with a purity higher than 99.9%, with
no presence of glassy phases according to observations made by means
of transmission electron microscopy (TEM). However, it is worth noting
that some second phases can be very useful, such as MgO as a sintering
aid in alumina to minimise the grain size [78] which plays an important
role in the decreasing wear rates of alumina with decreasing grain size
[75, 76]. Moreover, it is well known that the mechanical properties of
alumina-based ceramics depend on their purity, porosity, grain size and
grain distribution, but the machining processes involved must be
included since they should be accurate in order to optimise the surface

finish to avoid crack initiation [10]. In recent years, substantial
improvements in the manufacturing process have led to significantly
decreased rates of ceramic femoral head fracture, from more than 1%
in the 1970s to 0.004% in the 2000s [79, 80].
   However, although the efficacy with third generation alumina
ceramics was proved and available in the scientific literature, a small
risk of complications with the prostheses [3, 81, 82] still existed and
therefore, it was important to accelerate the development of alumina
ceramics with better mechanical properties. Nevertheless, there is no
doubt that the mechanical properties of the third generation of alumina
are outstanding compared to those required in the standard ISO/DIS
6474-1 [66]. A comparison of the mechanical properties required by
the mentioned standard and the third-generation alumina is shown in
Table 6.2 [55, 66]. However, and despite the excellent track record of
both safety and the long-term results using third-generation alumina
ceramics, they are being replaced in clinical practice by alumina matrix
composites (AMCs) composed of alumina and zirconia (zirconia-
toughened alumina—ZTA), according to reports by Affatato et al. [60]
and Masson [83].

Nowadays, in order to obtain a secure link between the alumina
insert and the acetabulum [84–88] the socket fixation methods have
been modified obtaining, as a result, the incorporation of a press-fit
metal-backed socket into the majority of contemporary alumina-on-
alumina in THA. Although these results have been favourable in
comparison with the conventional MoP articulation, the inconvenience
related to the lack of ductility of alumina ceramic can be an issue
regarding the risk of fracture during insertion or in vivo use [79, 89].
Recently, by using third-generation alumina, the reports show that the
fracture rate for currently available alumina femoral heads has been
reduced to a level of one fracture per 10,000 implants [17, 80, 84, 90].
However, we agree with what was expressed by Park et al. [84] in that
despite this extremely low rate, it may not be possible to eliminate the
actual risk of alumina head fracture, therefore patients should be
clearly informed of the potential risk for this severe complication
before receiving an alumina-on-alumina bearing. In light of this, the
incorporation of a polyethylene-alumina composite liner within a
titanium-alloy shell or, alternatively, a bioactive material as a coating on
the alumina to enhance primary fixation, has been investigated in an
attempt to address this problem [91, 92]. Nonetheless, this sandwich
liner has a high fracture rate and there is not sufficient evidence to
justify massive expenditure on advanced implants without having on
hand, real clinical data supporting their improved outcome compared
to traditional bearing surfaces currently in use [3]. Therefore, the great
challenge for ceramic engineering is to develop an improved material
which maintains all the advantageous properties of third-generation
alumina but allows new applications which require high mechanical
loading bearing capability [93] with increased toughness and hardness.
It is important to bear in mind the existence of an unpredictable
complication of hard-on-heard sliding surfaces as COC which is
referenced as squeaking [94]. The reported incidence of squeaking
varies considerably in the literature, at rates between 1 and 20% [95–
98]. However, squeaking is generally benign and does not lead to
revision. According to Tocks [99] and Own et al. [100], this
phenomenon could be caused by malposition of the acetabular
component with excessive inclination and anteversion, as well as loss of
the fluid film lubricating the joint, resulting in increased loading against

the edge of the cup. This behaviour is not exclusive to alumina ceramics
but is also observed in ZTA components and could be associated with
earlier generations of ceramic bearings, inasmuch as later generations
of these have been introduced with the aim to make the implant
stronger and more fracture-resistant. Today, there is no clear
conclusion about this unpleasant complication. However, multiple
studies have illuminated that various factors can play a role in the
formation of squeaking [101–103]. Taking in to account the
multifactorial nature of squeaking, these factors are integrated and
probably cannot be separated, and moreover, they can be classified
considering the patient characteristics, surgical factors, as well as
implant factors considering that this is a complication related to hard
on hard bearings and also of MoM that are catalogued as very sensitive
to component positioning. Based on the aforementioned, it is important
to evaluate in depth several factors such as patient, surgical, and
implant factors, and mainly the patient’s history in order to correctly
choose which type of ceramic prosthesis would have a better long-term
performance.

6.3 Zirconia Ceramics
In response to the concerns over in vivo fractures of Al2O3 femoral
heads and liners in THA in the 1980s [18, 104], yttria-stabilized
zirconia (Y-TZP) was introduced, and partially stabilized zirconia using
magnesia as well (Mg-PSZ) [105]. Due to its higher strength and
toughness [22], it was firstly called by Garvie “ceramic steel” [106].
Pure zirconia is a material showing three different crystalline phases:
monoclinic, tetragonal, and cubic [21]. The stabilisation of zirconia by is
reached with the addition of oxides such as MgO, CaO, CeO2 or Y2O3 to
control the phase stability of ZrO2, and to obtain several types of tough
ZrO2-containing ceramics [62, 107, 108]. This material was
standardised in 1997 (International Standard Organisation, ISO 13356)
and it is characterised by the t (tetragonal) to m (monoclinic) phase
transformation that may result in a net volume expansion of the surface
and subsurface grains, which is used to improve the mechanical
properties of ZrO2 ceramics such as PSZ and TZP by the mechanism of

transformation toughening [107–111]. This produces a reduction in the
stress intensity at the crack tip, generating a dissipation of the energy
of the propagating crack that must overcome both the energy required
for the material transformation and that associated with the volume
expansion of the transformed material [62]. Therefore, the sudden
volume change exerts compressive forces on the crack tip, thereby
slowing or arresting its propagation [18]. Y-TZP has about two to three
times larger fracture toughness and flexural strength than Al2O3,
making it one of the strongest ceramics for medical use [22].
Nevertheless, zirconia has very low thermal conductivity and for
biomedical use, it has the great inconvenience that femoral heads
should articulate only against polyethylene sockets since both zirconia
against alumina and zirconia against zirconia show catastrophic rates
of wear in vitro, according to the report by Willmann et al. [112].
     It is worth noting that a serious limitation of Y-ZTP is its tendency
to degrade in a moist atmosphere at temperatures between 150 and
400 °C (referred to as accelerated ageing, but it occurs at room
temperature too). Y-TZP may spontaneously transform to its stable
monoclinic form under in vivo conditions, which starts at the sample
surface resulting in microcracking and loss of strength [18]. This effect
is commonly known as low temperature degradation (LTD) or
hydrothermal ageing [113]. This phenomenon was first reported by
Kobayashi et al. [114] in 1981 and has been the subject of considerable
investigation [115–124] predicting, for example, failures from LTD in
the large number of zirconia implants used in the last decade
(>500,000) [22]. Moreover, the key findings of these studies were: (i)
the t to m phase transformation proceeds most rapidly at 200°–300 °C,
being time dependent; (ii) the transformation is favoured in a humid
atmosphere; (iii) a higher Y2O3 stabiliser content as well as finer grain
size improve the resistance to this transformation; and (iv) the
transformation starts at the surface and proceeds into the bulk,
degrading the ceramic. On the other hand, Chevalier et al. [125] have
clearly shown that LTD in Y-TZP also occurs far below 150 °C, including
the temperature used for steam sterilisation (~140 °C) and the human
body temperature (37 °C) [62].
   LTD is currently considered the Achilles’ heel of zirconia and the
overall process for its manufacture must be strictly controlled. Any

change in one of the process steps must be very carefully assessed
inasmuch as there is a precedent related to a change in manufacturing
methods (from batch to tunnel furnace) by the leading vendor of Y-TZP
in 1998 resulting in an alarming increase in fractures, beginning in
2000, with many occurring only months after implantation [126]. This
situation led to its withdrawal from the US and EU markets in 2001 and
its industrial standard was subsequently abandoned [18, 127].
However, nowadays, Y-TZP femoral heads are still available for
implantation in Asia, and its use may be limited and controlled through
improved processing and careful assessment before clinical use [128].
Under this scenario, Y-TZP is preferred as aesthetic and functional
dental prostheses [129], although some criticisms have also been raised
about its longevity in this application as a consequence of its LTD [130].
However, so far, there is no evidence of the LTD impact on clinical
outcome. Since the employment of 3Y-TZP in load-bearing applications
can lead to catastrophic fracture [62, 131] as well as surface
roughening [113], it is of paramount importance to estimate to which
extent an in vitro ageing test (standardised for biomedical grade ZrO2)
could be valid for predicting the in vivo resistance to LTD under ISO and
ASTM testing conditions [132]. As an example, Fig. 6.2 [133] shows
representative Raman spectra corresponding to a zirconia femoral head
before and after exposure to water vapour atmosphere (134 °C, 2 bars
of pressure) for 20 h. In the as-received state of the zirconia head, the
observed Raman bands indicate predominant spectral contributions
from the tetragonal phase (Fig. 6.2a), while the bands from the
monoclinic phase become the most preponderant after ageing for 20 h
(Fig. 6.2b). Likewise, representative optical micrographs of the head
surface are given in the upper right of each figure. As can be seen,
Fig. 6.2b reveals the homogeneous formation of transformation-
induced surface roughness with significant uplifts after autoclaving.
According to Arita et al. [133] the moisture-induced a slow t → m phase
transformation up to 5 h of ageing (Fig. 6.3), but it proceeded rapidly
after 7.5 h suggesting a behaviour which could be interpreted as a
nucleation/growth model according to studies by Chevalier et al. [113,
134], Johnson and Mehl [135], and Gremillard et al. [136].

     It is argued that the in vitro ageing time should theoretically be
comparable to the in vivo implantation periods. However, for a
conversion from in vitro to in vivo times following the activation energy
arguments, there is a clear discrepancy between ISO and ASTM criteria.
For medical grade 3Y-TZP, one-hour exposure at 134 °C under 2 bars
steam corresponds approximately to 4 years in vivo exposure,
according to ISO standard [134]. On the other hand, the standard ASTM
F2345-03 defined that one-hour exposure at the above condition
corresponds to 2 years in vivo [132], representing a more severe
condition for 3Y-TZP because of a shorter in vivo time for the same
ageing duration. An in-depth analysis of this context leads us to think
that in vitro ageing criteria should not be considered as rigorous and
universally true in lifetime extrapolation in vivo, but just as a rough
indication. Considering the fact that the most frequently published
studies to date refer to the ISO standard, Arita et al. [133] showed
without doubt that this standard is not the most appropriate to
evaluate the zirconia femoral heads for THA. In closing, with the
increased risk of catastrophic failure of zirconia femoral heads and
following an unusually high rate of clinical failures as a consequence of
alteration in manufacturing variables, Y-ZTP femoral heads were
withdrawn from orthopaedic applications in 2001 giving way to more
reliable materials.

6.4 Oxide Ceramic Composites
As mentioned above, Y-TZP [137] is well known to degrade both in vivo
and in artificial ageing tests due to the metastable tetragonal phase
transformation to the monoclinic phase in the presence of water [125,
138–140]. Inconveniences related to a series of Y-TZP femoral head
fractures in vivo [131, 141] led to a decrease in their use in the USA
with its standard being withdrawn in 2007. In order to overcome these
limitations, a new class of materials was developed in the nineties to
combine the tribological properties of alumina with the mechanical
characteristics of Y-TZP. These oxide ceramic composites, introduced in
the early 2000s, are referred to as alumina matrix composites [139] in

which Y-TZP is added to an alumina matrix to enhance its fracture
toughness. Zirconia toughened alumina (ZTA) is an alumina matrix
composite ceramic, in which alumina is the primary or continuous
phase (70–95%), and zirconia is the secondary phase (30–5%). These
composites have shown lower rates of wear in vitro comparable to
those of alumina ceramics [21].
   Highlighting the fact that most of the zirconia is retained in the
tetragonal phase, the addition of zirconia into the alumina matrix
results in higher strength and fracture toughness, decreasing hardness
as well as elastic modulus, in comparison to monolithic alumina
ceramics [142]. Currently, there are two main commercially available
ZTA biomaterials for THA applications: BIOLOX®delta (22.5 wt.% ZrO2,
76.1 wt.% Al2O3, and 1.4 wt.% chromium, strontium and others) by
CeramTec GmbH (Plochingen, Germany, currently on the market
worldwide), and the newest evolution from Kyocera AZUL (19 wt.%
ZrO2, 79 wt.% Al2O3, and 2 wt.% other) by KYOCERA Medical (Osaka,
Japan, available on the market in Japan). Since 2003 over 9.2 million
BIOLOX®delta femoral heads and over 2.7 million BIOLOX®delta
inserts have been produced. On the other hand, AZ209 was
commercially released by KYOCERA Medical in Japan during 2011.
BIOLOX®delta has shown improvements over previous ceramics such
as BIOLOX®forte [143, 144] in both the reduced numbers of fractures
[145] and reduced wear volumes [146]. This improved performance is
originated by a fine microstructure including well dispersed and
isolated sub-micron (~300 nm) particles of Y-TZP through the alumina
matrix [147].
   Pezzotti et al. [148] revealed results obtained by several
independent research groups showing some discrepancies between the
predicted in vitro and actual in vivo surface phase stability of
BIOLOX®delta (ZTA) femoral heads, suggesting a polymorphic
transformation [142, 149–152] considering thermodynamic
extrapolations of the in vitro hydrothermal model, according to a report
by Chevalier et al. [153]. In spite of the validity of the ASTM
standardised in vitro model [132], this could be a concern in its current
form; the data will call for a revision of the international standards after
obtaining more exact results [148]. An example showing this situation

can be seen in Fig. 6.4 where ZTA retrieval data corresponding to
different studies have also been rationalised on the same plot,
regardless of the articulating surfaces (i.e., CoC or CoP) [152, 154]. It is
important to stress that in spite of the observed consistency of the
slopes of Fig. 6.4, there is a serious discrepancy between the in vitro
and in vivo plots. Judging by the results, these suggest that in vitro low-
temperature simulation studies on the ageing of ZTA ceramics could
have some limitations when extrapolated to in vivo conditions.
However, the reality is that with over 15 million components since
2003, there is no evidence of LTD impact on clinical performance.
According to recent research work by Porporati et al. [154], it is well
known that there is a discrepancy concerning the evidence that in vivo
aged implants display a much higher monoclinic zirconia content than
expected from in vitro simulations by autoclaving zirconia-toughened
alumina (ZTA). The source of the discrepancy is not known although
some research groups invoke the effect of mechanical impact shocks
due to micro separation, which is not implemented in the ASTM in vitro
standard, or hip walking simulators, while others adduce the effect of
metal transfer, which should trigger an autocatalytic reaction in the
body fluid environment, accelerating the kinetics of tetragonal-to-
monoclinic transformation in vivo. The authors studied in depth the
origin of the existing discrepancy by using measurements on both in
vitro and in vivo aged BIOLOX®delta specimens and they demonstrated
that the Clarke/Adar equation, and not the Katagiri equation (see Refs.
[155, 156] in Porporati et al. [154], respectively) produced results that
are in better accordance with the XRD measurements suggesting that
this equation is the most suitable one to quantify the monoclinic
content in the investigated material with the used experimental setup
and showing also that metal transfer is not necessarily related to high
monoclinic content. However, previous studies showing the contrary
might be affected by the measurement methods leading to an
exaggerated monoclinic content. The results of the investigation [154]
revealed that the phase transformation toughening of the zirconia
phase in BIOLOX®delta has shown a significant positive impact on the
clinical setting with respect to monolithic alumina, not only in terms of
fracture rates, but also in terms of wear/ scratch/shock resistance.
Nguyen et al. [157] showed that the phenomena of phase

transformation occurs in BIOLOX®delta femoral heads implanted into
patients, where the amount transformed did not increase significantly
with the time that the femoral head had been implanted. On the other
hand, an important point is that the negligible effect upon burst
strength of the retrieved heads, as well as artificially aged heads
undergoing phase transformation, is reassuring and therefore, the
reported results support the continued clinical use of BIOLOX®delta as
a femoral head material for THA. Additionally, for the same material,
Clarke et al. [158] did not test enough samples to determine whether a
correlation between monoclinic zirconia content and burst load exists.
In light of this, it will be prudent to reproduce phase transformation
measurements and burst tests on longer-term retrieved heads as they
become available. In addition, there is a limitation referring to not
knowing the orientation of the retrieved heads while they were
implanted in the patients so limiting the ability to draw correlations
between the locations of applied loads in vivo and the locations of the
phase transformation.

   In ZTA composites, undoubtedly the Al2O3 matrix within the
microstructure is at least partly responsible for the small n exponent,
inasmuch as the transformation process is limited to isolated ZrO2
grains due to the constraining effects of the surrounding Al2O3 matrix.
Pecharromán et al. [159] recommended an upper limit of 16 vol.%
(~22 wt.%) for zirconia concentration in an alumina matrix in order to
avoid subsurface spreading of monoclinic domains. One possible reason
why the simulated results could be inadequate in predicting in vivo ZTA
transformation kinetics lies in that the effects corresponding to
mechanical stress induced by in vivo wear, impact, or shock, have not
been taken into account in the standard in vitro simulation test [148].
In fact, Perrichon et al. [160] suggested improving the protocol for in
vitro ageing of metastable ceramics which must include the effect of
surface stresses in evaluating their hydrothermal stability, emphasising
that it is not clear whether the presence of mechanical stress is the
main trigger for the enhanced in vivo transformation reported in
Fig. 6.4. Pezzotti et al. [148] reported a conclusion in their study related
with the inclusion in the protocol of the in vitro standard of the staining
of ZTA samples with transition metals since different studies have
demonstrated that they are extremely detrimental to surface
degradation, and the reality is that their presence on implanted femoral
heads is almost unavoidable inasmuch as femoral stems made of
transition metals strongly contaminate ZTA heads at the trunnion-head
interface due to high tensile stresses, and therefore, a proper
assessment of this concern is required. Nevertheless, Nguyen et al.
[157] do not have any proof of metal smearing related phase
transformation. By removing the metal smearing with chemical attack,
they did not measure any increase of m-ZrO2. There are now
controversial results about ZTA heads subjected to a severe
hydrothermal ageing test exhibiting a significant increase in monoclinic
phase concentration, as well as surface roughness, with no apparent
plateau observed. For example, Roy et al. [139] showed clinical studies
on retrieval specimens where the tetragonal-to-monoclinic phase

transformation occurred after just 2.7 years in vivo. They speculated a
correlation between surface roughness and monoclinic phase
concentration with continuous degradation in vivo, which in turn may
lead to stress concentrations and weakening of the ceramic implant
resulting in late fracture and wear. However, despite the fact that some
authors are claiming that the scientific track record of ZTA remains
limited [161], the large real world data show extremely low fracture
rates for BIOLOX®delta and extremely good clinical performance of
BIOLOX®delta [143].
   Mathys Ltd (Bettlach, Switzerland) proposed the alumina-
toughened zirconia (ATZ) with the brand name Ceramys as an
alternative to ZTA. This composite material is commonly composed of
80 wt.% Y-TZP and 20 wt.% alumina and is reported to have
outstanding mechanical and tribological properties [162]. ATZ
components have also been developed by Metoxit (Bio-Hips, Metoxit
AG, Thayngen, Switzerland), mentioning that Metoxit ATZ has gained
popularity in dental situations, but its use in orthopaedics is practically
non-existent. It is important to note that Bio-Hip is characterised by its
ability to withstand loads four times greater than conventional alumina
implants, but it is still not commercialised [163], whereas Ceramys was
commercialised in 2007 [161]. In this type of composites, the t-ZrO2 is
the matrix and Al2O3 is the minor phase and the strength
improvements in them are due to the transformation toughening
mechanism as well as intergranular crack deflection, which is induced
by the presence of the Al2O3 particulates at t- ZrO2 grain boundaries
[18, 164, 165]. Figure 6.5 illustrates that when a micro crack crosses
the zirconia matrix some of the ZrO2 particles will transform from
tetragonal (t) phase into monoclinic (m) crystalline phase structure
leading to an increase in volume, which in turn results in a local
compressive stress field surrounding the crack tip. Hence, under this
condition, the crack propagation will be inhibited resulting in enhanced
fracture toughness. The composites with high fracture toughness
belong in the system ATZ, while composites with high hardness and
relatively low fracture toughness belong to ZTA. It was observed that
the grain growth of alumina and zirconia during sintering determined
the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of ATZ and ZTA

composites [166, 167]. In this context, the dispersion of the Al2O3 and
ZrO2 grains is therefore an important design element to take in
consideration. However, these ATZ composites are also highly
susceptible to LTD because of the large proportion of t-ZrO2 grains,
although its kinetics is more retarded in comparison to Y-TZP ceramics
[168]. In spite of some controversial results reported in the scientific
literature, Begand et al. [168] reported positive results applying
different variants such as ageing temperature with variable soaking
times and vapour pressures, in order to evaluate the LTD resistance of
ATZ composites. These observations agree with the results of various
research teams where the tetragonal to monoclinic zirconia phase
transformation could be suppressed with additions >20 wt.% alumina
in a Y-TZP ceramic [169, 170]. However, the detection of a superficial
tetragonal to monoclinic phase transformation after the hydrothermal
treatments under different conditions is definite. Despite not
significantly influencing the strength, phase composition and surface
properties, these type of composites lead to some surface degradation
that could produce a decrease in reliability, and according to Yongqi et
al. [162], ATZ can be applied more specifically in dentistry because
artificial saliva in the ceramic surface sediments may be useful for
increasing the strength of the ceramics provided they do not present
defects that possibly affect their mechanical strength, which may lead
to early failure under the chewing load [171].

     It is of paramount importance to avoid the surface monoclinic
zirconia and for that, the presence of the dispersed alumina phase
within the zirconia matrix (ATZ composites) is decisive in achieving an
effective suppression of the hydrothermal degradation of these
composites. A previous study [172] showed, for the first time, the
formation of a protective layer of alumina on zirconia surface when the
ATZ/carbon nanotubes (CNTs) composite was sintered in the presence
of a graphite powder bed (to preserve the integrity of CNTs at the
sintering temperature). Under this context, the authors speculated that
CNTs dispersed into the ATZ composite promoted the formation of such
an alumina layer. On the other hand, taking into account this
experimental evidence, Estili et al. [172] undertook an investigation
with the purpose to determine if this protective alumina layer would be

formed when the ATZ composite, free of CNTs, is sintered in the
presence of a graphite powder bed and surprisingly it was found that
once again the in-situ formation of an alumina layer surrounding ATZ
pieces during sintering under the presence of graphitic compounds and
a low oxygen atmosphere, is evident. Therefore, this novel advance
made at the forefront of this field has had a high impact on the
materials science, since a classic disadvantage of ATZ ceramics starts to
be resolved, inasmuch as the presence of the surface monoclinic
zirconia phase could be completely avoided after severe age testing, in
other words, LTD can be brought down to a minimum. As an example,
Fig. 6.6 shows the microstructure of dense as-sintered surfaces of ATZ
(80 wt.% ZrO2 + 20 wt.% Al2O3) composites at 1520 °C for 12.5 h.

6.5 Non-oxide Ceramics
The use of oxide ceramics for artificial joints has been established. The
mechanical complications have been reduced and most of them are
rather due to mishandling [174]. In this context, silicon nitride (Si3N4)

has been proposed as an alternative to oxide materials. Silicon nitride is
a non-oxide ceramic with superior fracture toughness, relatively high
fracture strength and abrasion resistance, and used for high-
performance applications (heat exchangers, gas turbines, and
automotive engines) [175, 176]. This ceramic has shown to be
biocompatible, osteoconductive [177–180] with resistance to
hydrothermal degradation [174]. Currently, monolithic Si3N4 and
alternatively, ceramic-like silicon nitride coatings, are actively being
investigated as potential bearing materials for THA [181, 182] and knee
joints [16]. For these applications, low wear rate and low frictional
coefficients are required and Si3N4 sliding against itself, or metal, or
polyethylene, becomes ultrasmooth due to tribo-chemical polishing,
and friction becomes very low at increasing sliding distance, as
reported by Mazzocchi and Bellosi [183]. A great advantage of Si3N4 is
that it is radiolucent, so that both the implant and the underlying bone
can be visualised on plain radiography, a characteristic not possible
when metal implants are used [184]. Similar to ZTA, Si3N4 is non-
magnetic which enables magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
examination of soft tissues proximal to the implants with no artifacts. In
contrast, examination of soft tissue proximal to metal implants can be
problematic owing to the presence of MRI-related artifacts [185]. On
the other hand, Bal et al. [186] reported that from a mechanical
standpoint, Si3N4 easily exceed the demands placed on orthopaedic
bearings, whether articulating against PE, metal or Si3N4 itself.
Nevertheless, there are practical barriers to widespread adoption of
this technology, mainly related to the manufacture, such as material and
processing costs, the important need for reproducibility as well as
reliability, and the precision in manufacturing.
   Si3N4 (Silicon nitride) ceramics are commonly densified by
alternative techniques including supplementary means such as
nitridation of silicon powder, or with the application of pressure in
order to assist the sintering process, and therefore, to achieve near
theoretical density. These techniques can be summarised as follows: (i)
Reaction Bonding Silicon Nitride (RBSN), (ii) Hot Pressing Silicon
Nitride (HPSN), (iii) Sintering Silicon Nitride (SSN), (iv) Sintering
Reaction Bonding Silicon Nitride (SRBSN), (v) Hot Isostatic Pressing

Silicon Nitride (HIPSN), (vi) Hot Isostatic Pressing Reaction Bonding
Silicon Nitride (HIPRBSN), (vii) Hot Isostatic Pressing Sintered Silicon
Nitride (HIPSSN) and (viii) Hot Isostatic Pressing Sintered Reaction
Bonded Silicon Nitride (HIPSRBSN) [187–193]. Unfortunately, pure
dense silicon nitride ceramics are very difficult to produce by means of
conventional sintering (simple heating of powder compacts) owing to
the high degree of covalent bonding between silicon and nitrogen
[194]. It is important to point out that the densification by pressureless
sintering (conventional sintering) requires mass transport via volume
or grain boundary diffusion, and such diffusion is a thermally activated
process which requires a higher sintering temperature that would
result in a highly dense material. However, at high temperatures, Si3N4
starts to dissociate [194, 195]. Table 6.3 [184, 196] summarises the
main properties of Si3N4 ceramics obtained by different routes. All
these properties have made it suitable for a wide range of industrial
applications and clinical use since 2008. This ceramic has been used as
a fusion cage for arthrodesis of the cervical and thoracolumbar spine
[18, 197] with few reported adverse events [198]. However, extensive
testing of Si3N4 has indicated its potential as an articulation member as
well, but it must be regulated by the respective agencies for this
purpose [199].

The immuno-allergological compatibility of ceramic materials in
arthroplasty is frequently showed by clinical patient data, in vitro and
in vivo experiments, including safety assessment in terms of chromium
ion release.
   As mentioned earlier, THA is the standard treatment in which a
painful hip joint with arthritis is removed and replaced with an
artificial joint, often made from metal and plastic components, or
alternatively, ceramic materials. Moreover, this procedure is known for
excellent clinical results [1]. Since the early reports on patients with
cutaneous reactions to metal orthopaedic replacements in the 1960s

[2], hypersensitivity to metals (MHS) has been a serious preoccupation
for orthopaedic surgeons [3]. Because of this, there is the alternative of
using ceramic implants in those patients who suffer hypersensitivities
or suspected implant allergies. To assess the possible allergological
reactions with ceramic implants, the Clinic for Dermatology and
Allergology of the Ludwig Maximilians University, Munich [4]
performed in vitro and in vivo studies with the aim to evaluate mainly
whether there was any (allergic) patch test reaction to ceramic
materials in individuals with other allergies (e.g., also to metals) [3].
For this, patch testing was done on a consecutive series of 250 patients,
and was applied on the patient’s back using a European standard series
of 30 allergens (Hermal, Reinbek, Germany) supplemented by a
sterilised disc manufactured with alumina (Al2O3-BIOLOX®forte,
CeramTec, Plochingen, Germany), following the standard procedure on
days 3 and 4 [5]. None of the patients reacted to the BIOLOX®forte
discs, whereas nickel was the most frequent allergen with 17.2%
positive reactions [3].
   Regardless of the study on monolithic alumina (Al2O3-
BIOLOX®forte), it was considered very important to carry out a
subsequent series of experiments aimed to investigate the
allergological response of a ceramic composite material from the same
supplier (BIOLOX®delta, CeramTec, Plochingen, Germany). In fact, this
study was done because BIOLOX®delta contains chromium (the
included chromium is trivalent chromium strongly bound to the
alumina lattice), which is considered a potential elicitor of allergic
reactions. Therefore, it was important to know the possible existence of
a positive (allergic) patch test reaction to chromium-containing ceramic
material in individuals with a metal allergy. Similar to the results
obtained with Al2O3-Biolox®forte, nickel was the most frequent
allergen with 14.5% positive reactions, while none of the patients
reacted to the BIOLOX®delta discs.
   To complement these studies, the Bologna orthopaedic research
group at the Rizzoli Institute conducted a study to assess the potential
in vivo release of chromium ions from ceramic composite material
(BIOLOX®delta) bearings in arthroplasty patients [6]. The results of the
study show the respective chromium levels in vivo are comparable to

healthy individuals without THA. These results suggest that a release of
chromium ions is unlikely to happen due to the strong ionic interatomic
bonding of the chemical structure of BIOLOX®delta, confirming the
possibility of using it as an excellent alternative material to metal-based
bearing couples [7]. However, it is noteworthy that ceramic femoral
heads are substantially more expensive than those made of cobalt-
chromium alloys, commonly used in THA. However, studies by Kurtz et
al. [8] show that ceramic components are cost effective and prices are
getting closer to CoCr. An alternative option to ceramics are the
Oxinium (oxidised zirconium (OxZr)) implants (Smith & Nephew;
Memphis, Tenn) [9] with a composition of 97.5% zirconium/2.5%
niobium with the surface oxidised to zirconia, forming a metal/ceramic
composite [10]. Recent clinical comparison of Oxinium femoral
implants with alumina and zirconia ceramics replacements showed no
difference in immune response, including the response in revision
cases in which the Oxinium implants replaced ceramic components
placed for reasons of metal allergy [10]. Oxinium particulate is as inert
as zirconia and alumina ceramics and moreover, has the hypoallergenic
properties of these ceramics. Nevertheless, it is not suggested to revise
a ceramic bearing with an Oxinium component. The alumina particles
could heavily wear out the OxZr head. Taking into account that the
incidence of MHS appears to be increasing in general, and in the
surgical population given the general nature of allergic response to
nickel, cobalt, and other common metals in orthopaedic implants, it is
very likely that their use in orthopaedics will further increase because
of their hypoallergenic character [11].

For this important reason, it is imperative that physicians and
prosthetists alike understand the mechanical performance of the
different biomaterials currently available for total joint arthroplasty
and evaluate these materials in the context of joint mechanics. There is
a need to consolidate current information on the mechanical properties
of both established and novel biomaterials.
   An understanding of the properties of the different materials that
can be used in orthopaedic implants such as THA and TKA is essential
in the design and evaluation of such devices. This involves knowledge of
mechanical (strain, stiffness, hardness, yielding, fracture and fatigue

resistance), corrosion (surface chemical properties and chemical
reactions with the environment surrounding the orthopaedic devices)
and biological (the reaction of the body to the release of toxic
substances resulting from corrosion and wear in both the short and
long term) properties [1].

8.1 Metals
The mechanical properties of a specific implant depend not only on the
type of metal but also of the processes involved for the manufacture of
such a device. It is important to keep in mind that an appropriate
selection of the implant biomaterial is a key factor for long term success
of implants, and it must reduce the negative biologic response while
maintaining an adequate function. Due to complexity of this theme, we
make a great effort to summarise the most important mechanical
properties of the more commonly used metals in THA.

8.1.1 Strength
The diverse materials used for orthopaedic replacements, especially for
load bearing applications, must have excellent biocompatibility,
superior corrosion resistance in body environment, an optimal
combination of high strength and low modulus, high wear and fatigue
resistance, as well as high ductility and of course be without
cytotoxicity [2, 3]. Typically, the mechanical strength enables bone
tissue to withstand external forces and physiological loadings, and the
individual values can vary depending of the bone type, for example, the
compressive yield strength (YS) value ranges from 130 to 240 MPa and
the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) can be up to 280 MPa, according to
Chen and Thouas [4], Staiger et al. [5] and Gu and Zheng [6]. As an
example [4], the strength of long bones such as legs and arms vary
between 100 and 200 MPa, whereas for vertebrae it ranges between 1
and 10 MPa. As a principle and with the purpose to ensure long-time
durability of an orthopaedic implant, its strength should be like that of
the bone. However, an excessive strength can cause deterioration of the
surrounding bone. Conversely, an implant with poor strength is
doomed to fail in vivo [7]. The commonly used 316 L stainless steels
possess a YS of 210–280 MPa, while its UTS usually ranges between

540 and 1000 MPa [4, 8]. Nevertheless, these YS and UTS have been
increased with the recently developed BioDur 108 steel, with the YS of
600 MPa and UTS exceeding 900 MPa, which in turn is nowadays
considered as a promising alternative to 316L [9]. An increase in
strength could also be possible by improving the manufacturing
process. In steels the strength can be substantially improved by means
of cold deformation processing, and such a case is the UTS for the
BIOSSN4 steel which can be increased up to 1500 MPa under severe
cold processing [10].
  On the other hand, most of the CoCr-based alloys used in THA have
a YS > 500 MPa and a UTS ranging between 900 and 1540 MPa, values
comparable to the properties of the new generation of steels. Here
again the manufacturing process has a great influence on the resistance
of CoCr alloys since the strength is generally higher for wrought than
for cast work pieces [4]. The YS for cast Co–Cr–Mo used in biomedical
applications (ASTM F75) ranges from 450 to 520 MPa, while the UTS
lies between 650 and 890 MPa. On the other hand, forged Co–Cr–Mo
(ASTM F799) has YS levels between 900 and 1030 MPa and UTS levels
from 1400 to 1590 MPa. Higher values can be obtained after thermo-
mechanical processing in the other Co–Cr–Mo types alloyed with
elements such as W and Ni (e.g. ASTM F90 and F562). Likewise, the
highest YS value amongst all the materials used for THA and TKA, has
been reached by means of the cold processed and aged ASTM F562 Co–
Ni–Cr–Mo alloys (almost 1800 MPa) [11]. However, and in spite of these
high YS values, the highest specific strength amongst all the metal
biomaterials used in orthopaedic implants is observed in Ti-based
alloys.
     It is important to point out that titanium has been a major game
changer in the prosthetics industry [12]. Based on its benefits as well as
disadvantages, titanium is a significant metal in the orthopaedic field
that is worth building upon and improving. Aware of the shortage of
long-lasting implants, engineering is constantly working with the
purpose to create new alloys of certain metals that benefit the patient
[13]. There are numerous titanium alloy types used in orthopaedic
applications. In this context, the mechanical properties and strength
will depend, in great measure, on the chemical composition and phase
structure [9]. In general, these mechanical properties are comparable

to stainless steel, but they are lower than for Co-based alloys.
Depending on the impurity content, the YS value varies between 170
and 480 MPa, whereas its UTS varies from 240 to 550 MPa [4]. In the
case of Ti–6Al–4 V, its UTS can reach 930 MPa for similar vanadium-free
alloys, while the YS are typically between 795 and 860 MPa [4]. On the
other hand, β phase alloys commonly have a UTS from 600 to 1100 MPa
with the YS achieving similar maximum values. Niinomi et al. [9]
reported that the strength of Ti alloys increases with increasing oxygen
content and higher values can be obtained following various
treatments, such as solution treatment with subsequent ageing,
thermo-mechanical processing and severe plastic deformation (SPD)
technologies [11]. Typical examples of the optimisation of mechanical
properties by thermo-mechanical processing followed by solution
treatment and ageing process are the two most important β Ti alloys
used nowadays in orthopaedic implants, Ti–29Nb–13Ta–4.6Zr (wt. %)
alloy and the Ti–13Nb–13Zr (wt. %) alloy. It is of paramount
importance to stress that despite their advantages and promise, these β
Ti alloys have only found use in niche applications since their
extraction, processing, and alloying are directly associated with a high
cost according to studies by Kolli and Devaraj [14]. However, there are
still controversies regarding which is the best titanium alloy for
orthopaedic replacements. Regardless of the two Ti alloys mentioned
above, the Ti–6Al–4 V alloy is an optimal choice for THA due to its
excellent strength, flexibility, fixation as well as osseointegration, in
addition to its lightweight and adaptation to different body
temperatures and room temperatures [15].
   However, although the range of application of Ti-based alloys in the
medical field and orthodontic surgery is truly astonishing (joint
replacement parts for THA, TKA, shoulder, spine, elbow, to name a few
[2, 16], in general terms, the requirements of strength in these alloys
for biomedical applications are much lower and have received less
attention in the literature. Instead, they receive more attention
regarding properties such as modulus of elasticity, cytotoxicity,
corrosion resistance, and biocompatibility [14, 17, 18]. Table 8.1 [2, 4,
19–24] summarises the YS (stress which will cause a permanent

elements such as Mo, Ta, Nb, and Zr, their density is high. These alloying
elements are rare which leads to a high cost of raw materials. Moreover,
the high melting points required for manufacture cause segregation and
difficulty in preparation of these alloys [23, 30]. In light of this,
elements such as Fe, Mn, Sn, and Cr are being used in order to develop
new low-cost β-type Ti alloys with favourable mechanical properties for
biomedical applications [31, 32].

8.1.2 Wear
Over the years, different metals have been used in a variety of
applications in the medical field and more specifically in orthopaedic
implants [33]. Amongst the metals and alloys primarily used in
biomedical applications are stainless steels, Co alloys, and Ti alloys [34,
35]. It is well known that wear and corrosion are the primary reasons
for the failure of implant elements [36]. Regardless of some
applications of tribology in the biomedical field such as wear of
dentures [37], heart valves [38], plates as well as screws in bone
fracture repair [39], to name a few examples, it is without doubt that
the wear is the most important factor in controlling and determining
the long-term clinical performance of a metallic biomaterial as a
replacement which can be influenced by factors such as material
properties, conditions of the type of alloys developed, fabrication
processes, experimental test methods, and characterisation
methodologies, amongst others [36]. According to Prasad et al. [40], the
degradation of implants is initiated from mechanical wear of the
components as well as through electrochemical corrosive reactions
with body fluids, with mechanical wear being the most prominent in
MoM implants, and particularly in THA. Factors related to the patient's
life including its quality and quantity of synovial fluid, level and type of
stresses on articulating surfaces, material properties, geometry and
dimension, as well as the employed surgical technique, are of
paramount importance to take into account to evaluate the wear of the
components in contact with artificial joints [41, 42]. The abrasive,
adhesive, fatigue, and corrosive modes are considered the four types of
mechanism that may be implicated in the wear of metal components of
joint prostheses [43]. It is expected that adhesive wear would be the

most prominent in the MoM combinations, whereas abrasive wear is
catalogued as the predominant mechanism in the all cobalt-chromium
alloys where the socket of these prostheses also showed evidence of
considerable adhesive wear, while fatigue wear was noted on one
component according to the study by Walker et al. [44]. The prostheses
combinations can be MoM, CoC or MoP. In these combinations the
primary reasons for material related revision surgeries are aseptic
loosening, implant breakage, and wear of the acetabular, which amount
to 58% [45]. Today, mainly MoP, CoP and CoC are used whilst MoM is
banned.
   Wear in metallic orthopaedic joints occurs in four different modes.
An excellent approach to the wear modes is described by Seyyed
Hosseinzadeh et al. [46]: “Mode 1 wear results from the motion of two
primary bearing surfaces one against each other, as intended. Mode 2
refers to the condition of a primary bearing surface moving against a
secondary surface, which is not intended. Usually, this mode of wear
occurs after excessive wear in mode 1. Mode 3 refers to the condition of
the primary surfaces moving against each other, but with third body
particles interposed. In mode 3, the contaminant particles directly abrade
one or both of the primary bearing surfaces. This is known as three-body
abrasion or three-body wear. The primary bearing surfaces may be
transiently or permanently roughened by this interaction, leading to a
higher mode 1 wear rate. Mode 4 wear refers to two secondary
(nonprimary) surfaces rubbing together”. The Fig. 8.1 clearly illustrates
these wear modes.

   Keeping in mind that the wear resistance of a metallic replacement
is clinically very important, several studies have been performed in
order to investigate their tribological properties. For this, different
wear test methods have been used by various researchers to

the wear and friction of different metallic biomaterials using a suitable

methods most commonly used to study the tribological behaviour of
metallic biomaterials are the block-on-disc [47, 48], ball-on-disc [49–
52], and pin-on-disc [53] where such tests are commonly conducted in
an environment of simulated body fluids (Ringer’s solution) [47], or

   The great variety of investigations concerning the wear of
biomedical implants have demonstrated that although the most
common type of hip joint comprises femoral head articulating against
an UHMWPE acetabular cup, MoM prostheses produce 20–100 times
lower wear volumes compared to MoP bearings [56]. For example,
McGee et al. [57] noted that titanium alloy femoral heads consistently
had the maximum wear, averaging 74.3% against UHMWPE acetabular
components. In this context there is a resurgence of the MoM bearings
instead of MoP, however, these produce nanometre-to submicrometric
sized metal particles [58, 59] which lead to a large cumulative surface
area for corrosion, inducing pathological changes that are associated
with hypersensitivity and osteolysis [60, 61]. With the purpose to

overcome this wear related and hence, the revision surgery, there has
been continuous effort to replace the cup material from polymer to
metal or ceramic, thus, the long-term problems associated with
UHMWPE wear debris have led to the exploration of the use of MoM
prostheses. It was observed [2, 62] that the biological reaction to metal
particles in vivo is markedly different to that produced by UHMWPE
wear debris, and lower inflammatory reactions are caused by metal
[63]. In spite of MoM prostheses exhibiting higher frictional torques
than the MoP [64], the problem remains latent for the effect of the
metal particles released after long durations [2].
   The optimum material combinations to give the lowest wear rates
coupled with the greatest host tolerance to the wear particles remains a
challenge. Considering the options MoP or MoM, currently there is not
definite evidence to favour one or the other, although MoM has been
proven to be a disaster. However, there is evidence that cobalt-
chromium particles may be more harmful than those of polyethylene
[43, 65, 66]. Moreover, neither stainless steel against itself nor titanium
against itself should provide a low-wear rate, low-friction system
because of their tendency to gall and seize [43]. Inevitably, wear debris
generates at all sliding interfaces owing to the relative motion of the
implanted components (between polymers, ceramics, and metals)
inasmuch as all the materials have a certain finite roughness [11]. What
is a reality is that wear for MoM and metal-on-ceramic (MoC) designs is
far lower than at interfaces with polymers; therefore, the largest
amount of debris is generated by polymers sliding against metals and
ceramics. The CoC designs exhibit a volumetric wear rate of
approximately 0.04 mm3/year, while the rate for the best MoM design
was 0.9 mm3/year [67]. Wear rates for polymer-metal hip implant
systems were reported to be between 4.5 mm3/year and 78 mm3/year
[67–69]. It is important to stress that in vitro, CoM has also been
banned.
   Considering that MoM are the bearing couples more used in THA,
[59, 60, 62, 70–73], wear in MoM bearings can result in scratching and
eventually erosion of the material, thus, wear and corrosion are very
probably the major causes of release of metal into the tissues of MoM
patients. Based on the mean time in situ, an annual wear rate of
7.6 mm/year (range, 2.9–13 mm/year) was calculated for the bearing

combinations. Likewise, also based on the implants’ time in situ, the
mean volumetric wear rate was 2.02 mm3/year (range, 0.55–3.74
mm3/year). Now, with a density of the alloy of 8.38 g/cm3, the mean
gravimetric wear rate was calculated to 17 mg/year (range, 4.6–
31 mg/year) [70]. On the other hand, it is believed that the linear wear
rates are dependent on a multitude of factors such as the type of
implant and positioning, according to reports by Onda et al. [74],
Shimmin et al. [75], and Williams et al. [76]. Table 8.3 presents an
excellent collection of various developed materials and their
manufacturing techniques, the types of wear tests carried out, as well

techniques to improve the tribological properties of metal
replacements, altering the nature of its surface by applying modern
concepts of surface engineering [41] such as ion implantation (physical

techniques used to enhance surface hardness, which in turn improves
the wear resistance of different metallic alloys, and plasma spray
coating to enhance the wear resistance of a few biomaterials, to
mention some [36].

8.1.3 Fatigue
In modern medicine, the use of metallic implants is more and more
important [89]. Fatigue fracture as well as are some of the major
problems associated with implant loosening, stress-shielding, and
ultimate implant failure [90, 91]. It is well known that under diverse
physiological conditions, orthopaedic implants are subjected to a very
complex interaction of mechanical and chemical–biological loading
components [92] where the cyclic loads, which have to be sustained in a
very corrosive medium containing enzymes, proteins and cells, are one
aspect of the in vivo loading scheme. Generally, fatigue takes place
when repetitive cyclic loading on the implant weakens the surface
leading to the production of cracks, irremediably causing fragmentation
and pitting, including in some cases, gouges, etches, surface
discolouration, surface deposits and third-body particulate generation
[40, 93]. Additionally, Teoh [90] and Geetha et al. [2] reported the
occurrence of fatigue failure of hip implants when they are subjected to
cycles of loading and unloading over many years. In this context, it is
likely that the majority of mechanical failures occurring in orthopaedic

implants during use are fatigue failures, and that it is equally probable
that the saline environment influences this fatigue behaviour. For the
case of metallic joint replacements, this has to transmit load unaided by
bone and so the occurrence of fatigue failures is far more serious [43].
However, and even after several years of widespread clinical use in
THA, few reports related to mechanical failures have been reported
because the conditions under which these failures occur are not clear.
Nevertheless, in spite of reports by Ducheyne et al. [94] describing
eight cases where everyone involved a prosthesis in a valgus position, a
more in depth study is required in order to determine an approach
conducive to understanding the mechanisms that cause the
catastrophic failure by fatigue of the metallic prosthesis. In general,
failures have been reported in stainless steel, cobalt-chromium alloys,
as well as titanium and titanium alloys.
     It is worth noting that together with wear, fatigue is among the most
harmful phenomena which can result in the ultimate failure of
orthopaedic implants [11, 90]. The fatigue strength, which is related
with the maximal cyclic stress before the occurrence of any damage or
failure, depends principally on the microstructure, surface quality of
the component, and the loading conditions [4, 90]. It usually initiates in
the most highly stressed location, and therefore, is especially dangerous
since it can occur before the stress level reaches the UTS and even the
YS, without any warning. It is important to differentiate between
fretting fatigue (hip joints mainly) that occurs when the cyclic stress
combines with the influence of friction, and fatigue that is supported by
the effects of corrosion and commonly referred as corrosion fatigue [4].
Recent premature failures of metal THA have raised concerns in the
medical community about their load bearing capacity, safety, reliability,
and survival rates, inasmuch as specifically, the femoral stem fracture is
one of the most acute complications resulting in greater morbidity and
higher cost of revision hip surgery. However, Nganbe et al. [95]
reported an unusual case of fatigue failure of a cobalt-chromium alloy
cementless femoral stem after 24 years of excellent performance,
where the failure occurred at the neck-stem junction remote from any
modular interface, and the fractographic studies and microstructural
investigations revealed no intrinsic defect of the failed component. This
behaviour illustrates the importance of proper long-term testing of

implants in regard to cyclic loading since today the patients are
younger and more active, and therefore, these implants must guarantee
a long-term fatigue resistance. Despite numerous investigations on the
fatigue strength of common metallic implant alloys used in orthopaedic
applications, such as stainless steel, cobalt, and titanium alloys, the
occurrence of failures caused by fatigue is still a major problem [96–
98]. Microstructural characterisations have shown a broad spectrum of
characteristics on fracture surfaces of failed implants, such as
intergranular/transgranular cracking, fatigue striations, and cleavage
or cleavage like surface topography. In the scientific literature there are
numerous results of fatigue strength in metals commonly used in
orthopaedic replacements which can vary depending on the technique
used to characterise such fatigue strength [86, 89, 95, 96].
   In the field of metals used for implants, for example, the fatigue
strength of as-cast stainless steels in aqueous biological solutions is
usually between 200 and 300 MPa [4, 11], this being acceptable for
most applications within the human body. Nevertheless, these values
can be improved via subsequent deformation processing and/or by
nitrogen content increase. Likewise, the fatigue strength of forged 316L
steel (steel most commonly used metallic material in orthopaedic
implants) was reported to reach 400 MPa according to investigations by
Teoh [90]. Nonetheless, Co-based alloys generally have higher fatigue
strengths than stainless steels, and taking into account this advantage,
CoCr alloys are a suitable choice for applications for cyclically loaded
prostheses and any highly loaded component reaching fatigue
strengths > 500 MPa, or alternatively, 700 MPa reached by means of
modern powder metallurgy (PM) techniques such as Hot Isostatic
Pressing (HIP) [90]. However, the processing route influences the
fatigue strength of these Co-based alloys, obtaining a value as low as
100 MPa for cast and 200 MPa for mechanically processed components.
Continuous investigations have led to improvements in casting
methods, inspection, and machining techniques to significantly increase
the fatigue strength of Co-based alloys. Thanks to these improvements,
implants manufactured from the Co-based alloys now enjoy a wide
acceptance throughout the medical world since a great deal of data has
been accumulated from both research and clinical studies that justifies
much of the confidence in applying these type of alloys in orthopaedics

[99]. However, an important observation must be taken into account,
which is the fact that these implants experience a severe cyclic loading,
negatively affecting their fatigue performance for the specific case of
cast and forged Co alloys under simulated body fluids, which can be the
cause of the low success of THA after 20 years [4, 100].
   Indeed, the fatigue resistance of forged Co-based alloys is
considerably higher than that of cast alloys, the fatigue strength of
forged Co–Cr being > 600 MPa (in air), whereas for cast Co–Cr, it is
approximately 300 MPa [4, 90, 101]. The fatigue behaviour of Co-based
alloys for orthopaedic implants can be improved by controlling the
alloy composition, and via heat treatment [102]. For example,
Hernandez-Rodriguez et al. [100] increased the fatigue resistance in the
as-cast condition of Co-based alloys via the addition of boron (B) and
they observed a fatigue resistance of 615 MPa for the alloy with 1 wt. %
B, representing an improvement of 60% regarding the base alloy.
Conversely, heat treatment diminished the fatigue resistance of most
alloys containing B, except the 0.06 wt. % B, which retained its fatigue
resistance at the same level of 433 MPa, as observed in the as-cast
condition. Moreover, continuous investigations have demonstrated that
by means of surface treatments [11], the fatigue strength and other
properties of the Co-based alloys can be significantly improved, as will
be described later on.
   Concerning titanium alloys, the Ti–6Al–4 V (Ti64) alloy is still the
most commonly used α+β titanium biomedical alloy and is used under
the annealed condition whereas the metastable biomedical alloys are
preferred in the solution treated (ST) and, ST and aged conditions [2]. It
is important to remember the urgent need to find more reliable
materials, metals, and mainly ceramics, to replace broken or
deteriorating parts of the human body due to the rapid increase in the
number of both younger and older recipients. In this context, there is a
necessity to obtain metals and alloys of extreme chemical inertness and
adequate mechanical strength [103, 104]. Therefore, the medical
community has found an opportunity with the use of titanium and its
alloys in orthopaedic replacements such as THA and TKA, taking
advantage of their excellent corrosion resistance, a high strength to
weight ratio, and low elastic modulus [105]. Regardless of the material
used in orthopaedic implants design, the presence of geometrical fillets

such as notches, which cause local stress, is unavoidable and therefore,
it is necessary to pay attention to these notches, considering that they
affect the fatigue resistance [106]. Due to this, the failure frequently
takes place as a result of high tensile stresses at the surface or around
notches (for example drill holes in intramedullary nails or plates)
[107]. Another important point to take into account is the
interdependency between factors such as implant shape, material,
processing technique, as well as the type of cyclic loading, making the
determination of the fatigue resistance of a component an intricate, but
critical task, according to the report by Hosseini [103].
   The titanium alloy Ti–6Al–4 V is generally considered as a standard
material when evaluating the fatigue resistance of orthopaedic titanium
alloys. However, its mechanical response is extremely sensitive to its
prior thermo-mechanical processing history (prior β grain size, the
ratio of primary α to transformed β, the α grain size, the α/β
morphologies, surface preparation) which especially impacts the high-
cycle fatigue lifetime (HCF) [103]. In fact, enhancement of the HCF
resistance of Ti–6Al–4 V may be achieved, under careful control, by
shot peening [103] where, under a cold working process, the surface is
bombarded with typically spherical media so plastically deforming the
surface and then the resulting compressive residual stresses may
provide an increased part life when the surface related failure
mechanisms, such as fatigue or corrosion, are involved [108]. However,
to guarantee the optimum performance, a perfect balance between, on
the one hand, the high compressive surface residual stresses and on the
other hand, the increased surface roughness produced during shot
peening, must be achieved. This surface treatment increases the fatigue
strength of Ti–6Al–4 V by 10% over grit blasting alone. The effect of
different surface finishing techniques on the fatigue strength of both α
and α/β titanium alloys is illustrated in Table 8.4 [103, 109]. According
to Dowling [110], the denominated fatigue notch factor Kf, (Table 8.4) is
affected by the notch radius (ρ). Specifically, when Kf = 1, there is no
degradation in the component due to the notch, whereas if the notch
has a large radius (ρ) at its tip, then Kf may be essentially equal to Kt
(stress concentration factor which depends upon the geometry of the
notch and the loading mode, and is defined by the maximum local

stress (σmax) to nominal stress (σnom) ratio) [111] and in this scenario
the notch produces the full theoretical reduction in the fatigue limit.
However, it is important to highlight that owing to the complexity
involved, empirical estimates are commonly used to obtain Kf values
which are used in design of orthopaedic replacements [110].

an actuator in the test machine at every 50,000 load cycles) values
whereas the solid implants showed a lower displacement compared to

the lightened ones, corroborating that the solid implants have a higher
stiffness than the lightened ones.
