     It has been mentioned previously that additions of small amounts of
MgO (<0.25 wt.%) in pure alumina for the preparation of femoral heads
promotes the control of grain growth leading to a completely dense and
strongly fine homogeneous structure. Azhar et al. [364] observed that
the addition MgO to ZTA can improve the hardness. However, Arab et al.
[365] found that MgO additions sacrifice the fracture toughness,
decreasing it from 4 MPa m1/2 for pure ZTA to 3.02 MPa m1/2 for ZTA
with the addition 0.9 wt. % MgO in conventionally sintered composites.
This suggests that the small grain size of ZTA samples affects the
fracture toughness due to the decreased load bridging capability of
smaller grain bridges [366] which, in turn, will be unfavourable for
orthopaedic applications. Other researchers have reported a variety of

fracture toughness values for pure ZTA composites. These include
Couto et al. [367] who reported 4.2 and 4.6 MPa m1/2 for pure ZTA
composites, pressureless sintered at 1500 and 1600 °C, respectively,
Ning and Ren [368] who obtained 6.55 and 8.42 MPa m1/2 in Al2O3 + 
15%ZrO2 and Al2O3 + 25%ZrO2 composites prepared by hot pressing
(HP), respectively, and Oungkulsolmongkol et al. [369] who reported
3.50, 3.70, 4.24 and 4.55 MPa m1/2 for alumina with ZrO2 contents of
10, 20, 30, and 40 vol% respectively, conventionally sintered in air
atmosphere at 1600 °C for 2 h.
   As can be summarised from the mentioned fracture toughness
values, there are numerous options to investigate in depth the
performance of ZTA composites for orthopaedic applications. In fact, a
large number of fracture toughness values previously mentioned, and
others not reported here, are greater than the value of 5.8 MPa m1/2
reported for ZTA BIOLOX®delta, which represents the most recent
advance on the market for orthopaedic applications, providing
advantages of the previous generation of alumina ceramics along with
innovative toughening mechanisms. This ZTA composite is today the
one most used throughout the world, mainly in THA [370]. Now, taking
advantage of the excellent mechanical properties obtained with ZTA
BIOLOX®delta, the scientific and orthopaedic community has
undertaken preliminary studies based on the addition of multi-wall
carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) to ceramic matrices for possible and
special applications such as implant materials [279, 348, 371, 372],
since preliminary biocompatibility tests [371] have indicated that the
composites showed no cytotoxicity to human osteoblast cells. In this
context, Akin [371] reported a fracture toughness of 5.5 MPa m1/2 for
the ZTA composite (30 vol% Y-TZP) with additions of 0.5 wt. %
MWCNTs prepared by SPS at 1400 °C under 40 MPa for 5 min. Despite
the promising results, there is the strong necessity for more detailed
understanding of the relationship between carbon nanotubes (CNTs)
and ceramic matrices in order to obtain the properties required by
international standards for orthopaedic applications.
     It is well known that in both ZTA and ATZ composites, the fracture
toughness of the ceramic matrix is increased in comparison to their
monoliths. However, for quite a long while, ATZ composites have been

utilised for wear parts and cutting apparatus, taking advantage of their
high quality, hardness, sturdiness, and abrasion resistance [288, 373–
375]. The few investigations carried out to improve the mechanical
properties of ATZ composites as joint replacements have shown
promising fracture toughness values. For example, several years ago
Chaim [376] reported a fracture toughness of 9 MP m1/2 (measured by
SENB method) for the ZrO2 + 20 wt. % Al2O3 composite, pressureless
sintered at 1650 °C for 4 h. Sadangi et al. [377] obtained a fracture
strength of 3.98 MPa m1/2 in ZrO2 + 40 wt. % Al2O3 prepared by CIP at
200 MPa and subsequently HIPed at 1400 °C under 200 MPa applied
pressure for 2 h, Faga et al. [378] investigated ZTA and ATZ reporting a
fracture toughness value of 7.1 MPa m1/2 for the composite ZrO2 + 20
wt. % Al2O3 CIPed at 200 MPa and conventionally sintered at 1500 °C
for 2 h, and Li et al. [379] sintered a composite of ZrO2 + 20 wt. % Al2O3
using SPS, reaching a fracture toughness of 5.27 MPa m1/2. More
recently, Gil-Flores et al. [380] obtained dense ATZ nanocomposites (20
wt. % Al2O3) densified by nonconventional microwave sintering
technology at temperatures of 1200 and 1300 °C, reporting a fracture
toughness of 5.7 MPa m1/2. Meanwhile, a composite with the same
composition but densified under conventional sintering at 1500 °C for
2 h showed a fracture toughness of 5.5 MPa m1/2. These results
regarding fracture toughness are influenced by the sintering
mechanisms and methods which are reflected in the final properties
and microstructure of the obtained composites [360, 378, 381, 382].
Taking into account the fracture toughness values for ZTA and ATZ
composites, generally, an increase of fracture toughness is observed
when zirconia particles are added to the alumina matrix whereas a
decrease in the fracture toughness is noticeable with the addition of
alumina particles into the zirconia matrix. Therefore, to fulfil the
requirements of the composite for orthopaedic applications, it is of
paramount importance to find an adequate balance in the specific
properties with the aim of reaching an optimum performance of the
material.
   Apart from the aforementioned oxide ceramics which have been
used for several years, there is silicon nitride that is now one of the
most extensively studied ceramics in history and as its properties are

now well understood, its commercial use has expanded greatly [337] in
applications such as high-performance bearings, turbine blades and
glow plugs, as well as in industrial applications where extreme strength
and toughness are necessary [383]. In this sense, the predominant
properties of Si3N4 have led to speculation that it can play an
outstanding role in biomedical fields since it is biocompatible [384,
385] and has already been used in spinal fusion implants [337]. This
material has the peculiarity that its fracture toughness can be improved
by an “in-situ toughening” thermal treatment by means of HIP method
at temperatures higher than 1700 °C, reaching fracture toughness
values approaching 10 MPa m1/2 in comparison to values of ~3 MPa
m1/2 for the same material composition with less elongated sub-
micrometre diameter grains [386, 387]. However, practical barriers to
widespread adoption of this non-oxide ceramic relate to the material
and processing costs, as well as the need for reproducibility, reliability,
and precision in manufacturing. The fracture toughness values reported
in the scientific literature are very varied considering that the
mechanical properties of Si3N4 are very dependent on the additives
used to reach full densification at high temperatures, such as Y2O3,
Al2O3, La2O3, and MgO, amongst others. Generally, and independently of
the equation used for the determination of the fracture toughness of
Si3N4, Kim et al. [388] reported a fracture toughness of 4.66 MPa m1/2
for the composition Si3N4 + 3% Al2O3 + 8% Y2O3 using the indentation
fracture method, Lu and Huang [389] obtained 11.80 MPa m1/2 with
the Single-Edge Pre-cracked Beam (SEPB) method in the composition
Si3N4 + 6% Yb2O3 + 2% Al2O3, and Wang and Mao [390] and
Carrasquero Rodriguez et al. [391] reported a value of 8.06 MPa m1/2
for the composition Si3N4 + 5% Al2O3 + 2.5% Y2O3 + 7.5% La2O3 by
means of the Chevron-Notched Beam (CNB) method. In short, there are
a wide range of fracture toughness measured values for different
advanced ceramics which could be used in the orthopaedic field.
However, more in-depth investigations are needed to reach the optimal
efficiency when these materials are used in orthopaedic implants.

8.2.4 Fatigue

Fatigue fracture as well as wear, are two of the major problems
associated with implant failure of some medical devices which are
frequently reported in orthopaedic applications such as THA. While it is
impossible to avoid failure, recent investigations have focussed on
predictive tools in order to enable more accurate predictions aimed to
prevent catastrophic failure in vivo [90].
  When ceramic components are used in orthopaedic applications,
long-term reliability is a major concern [392, 393] which occurs below
the critical failure strength and is a common phenomenon in metals
and ceramics. Grathwohl and Liu [394] reported the existence of cyclic
fatigue effects in ceramics, and experimental evidence was reached for
a limited range of experimental. Nowadays, there is a strong demand
for the generation of design-relevant fatigue data because the present
knowledge of fatigue in ceramic materials is insufficient [395–397]. The
application of fatigue tests to the brittle materials imposes a number of
problems, the main one being the wide scatter in data due to the defect
distribution in the samples and which sometimes complicates the
results. [398]. In spite of the aforementioned, it is generally observed
that the surface damage in THA is a result of a fatigue process [46]
since they undergo cyclic loading for a fairly long period in a corrosive
environment. For fatigue studies, the relation between the stress
intensity factor KI and the crack velocity V can be used for the
characterisation of the subcritical crack growth (SCG) for the fatigue in
alumina and zirconia, where the KI–V characteristics are parameters
used for their lifetime predictions based on fracture mechanics [399].
However, the fatigue lifetime prediction may not have been determined
for zirconia, in particular [400, 401], in comparison to many studies of
fracture behaviour by fatigue for other bio-ceramics, for example Refs.
[402, 403].
   For the specific case of alumina, Basu [404] carried out an
interesting investigation on fatigue behaviour of fine-grained alumina
femoral heads (a high-pure variety of alumina powder with additions of
0.25% MgO as a grain growth inhibitor) under normal walking
conditions, considering that for application of alumina in THA,
reliability is an essential prerequisite and therefore, the mechanical
behaviour of this material for a period ranging between 20 and
30 years is of paramount importance. In this research, cyclic stress was

directly applied on small femoral heads made of alumina with the aim
to simulate a normal hip-joint during walking, and to generate a very
low polyethylene wear rate. Static fatigue behaviour of alumina under
constant load was studied on a 4-point bending fixture and the
specimens were loaded at the rate of 22 N/s up to a predetermined
level. During the operation, the instrument was kept under load control
mode. On the other hand, cyclic fatigue was studied under a sinusoidal
stress wave form where a stress ratio of 0.5 was maintained with a
frequency of 5 Hz, where the mean value of the cyclic stress was kept
identical with the value of the static stress. In another scenario, the
cyclic fatigue of the femoral heads is basically a fatigue-testing machine
equipped with software which measures the stress on the test piece
which is equivalent to the actual stress experienced by a natural human
hip-joint, in various postures. Basu [404] concluded that to provide a
fatigue life of more than 40 years, the alumina heads should have cracks
below a specific dimension as well as the capacity to withstand a
compressive load around of 30 kN. It is noteworthy that a set of tests
would be necessary to check the reliability of the performance of these
heads when a sudden compressive load of 30 kN is imposed on them. If
these samples pass the test, they would undoubtedly serve for at least
40 years in a patient of 400 kg body weight, since this would mean that
on the one hand that the samples withstood the test parameters for 107
test cycles and on the other hand, the samples resisted the maximum
walking stress of 17.2 kN which is equivalent to a body weight of
400 kg. However, it is important to keep in mind that THA does not only
refer to a femoral head, but there are other components that could fail
prematurely so shortening the life of the implant. The mentioned data
suggest that modern Al2O3 bearings can be safe and reliable if these are
used with THA components with proven design and durability.
Nevertheless, in spite of that, the risk of failure is still unacceptably high
[265]. Commonly, the failure of ceramic bearings in vivo results from
subcritical crack growth (SCG) under the static or repetitive loading
experienced in the body, until fracture occurs [405].
    Specifically, alumina ceramics are prone to experience SCG
subcritical crack growth, [406, 407]. In other words, imperfections such
as pores, inhomogeneities and scratches, as well as micro-notches
(cracks) in the material or on the surface lead to stress concentrations

upon exposure to load. With this regard, it is important to note that the
speed of crack propagation,     , under tensile load, σ, can be described

However, this appreciation leads to the minimisation of structural

and moreover, the evaluation of the data may be complicated [413].
   However, and perhaps because of the wide use of zirconia in
femoral heads some years ago, there are more reports related with SCG
in zirconia ceramics. For example, Wojteczko et al. [414] following the
same procedure as used for alumina, reported an n parameter of
approximately 28.30 for 3Y-TZP sintered at 1500 °C for 2 h. In spite of
controversial reports on the exact reasons of zirconia head failure, the
common outcome of all the studies done so far is that more research is
needed to elucidate the reason of that failure [415]. The initial non-
critical microcracks and other defects led to the fatigue of the material
with a final catastrophic fracture of the femoral head. Undoubtedly, the
changes in the manufacturing process and parameters related to the
patient have a great influence for the increase in failure rates of zirconia
femoral heads [416]. Up to now, the accurate mechanism of failure
remains speculative and a common opinion in the recent literature
leads to that the ISO criteria should be expanded with the purpose to
provide high quality standards for applications in THA [354].
   In zirconia mainly, the analysis of SCG can be difficult due to the
effect of transformation toughening on crack velocities. However, and
according to Chevalier et al. [417], a large number of studies have
focussed on SCG in zirconia-based composites but only a few  –KI
curves have been obtained for a large range of crack rates. For
conventional 3Y-TZP, Zhu et al. [399] found an n parameter of 21.8 and
17.6 in air under static and cyclic loading conditions, respectively. On
the other hand, this n parameter decreased in water to 21.5 and 15.2 in
static and cyclic loading conditions, respectively. From these results, it
is observed that the crack propagation parameter n in zirconia is clearly
smaller than that in alumina, as well as that the crack velocity in

zirconia is higher than that in alumina in both environments of air and
water. Although the increase in the crack velocity in a water
environment is observed in both materials, this increase is more
remarkable for zirconia. In another investigation, Chevalier et al. [418]
found a value for n of about 32 for 3Y-TZP ceramics with grain sizes of
0.3, 0.5, and 1.0 µm, whereas Knechtel et al. [419] found an n value of
29 for Y-TZP.
   Regardless of the material used in the manufacture of the femoral
head (alumina, zirconia, ZTA or ATZ), this must achieve extraordinary
reliability over a long period of time, preferably 20–50 years. To reach
this goal, an efficient alternative is to make a calculation of the lifetime
of ceramic heads based on experimental fatigue and slow crack growth
tests using finite element analysis [420]. As mentioned previously, Y-
TZP was successfully used in orthopaedics for more than 10 years until
the serious problem caused by its high fracture rate in 2001 (Y-TZP
under the commercial name Prozyr by Saint Gobain Ceramiques
Desmarquest). Drouin et al. [420] undertook investigations on SCG of
commercial zirconia ceramic femoral heads (PROZYR®) under static
and cyclic loading following the FDA guidelines, before they were
recalled from the market [265]. The study was carried out at very low
crack velocity (< 10−11 ms−1) under static and cyclic fatigue by means of
a double torsion technique. For static fatigue, the results showed the
existence of a threshold value of stress intensity factor of approximately
3.5 MPa m1/2 below which crack growth is absent. It is very interesting
to mention that the scientific literature (for example Ref. [421]) had
already mentioned the existence of this threshold but this was never
experimentally determined for polycrystalline ceramics. By then, this
threshold represented one of the most outstanding advantages of
zirconia compared to other ceramics used in the field of orthopaedics
which would lead to a remarkably strong enhancement of implant
lifetime. On the other hand, the SCG has shown that it is influenced by
cyclic loading which shortens the lifetime, whereas the crack growth
rate is significantly increased when is compared to quasistatic loading,
according to studies by Liu and Chen [422]. Similar to static fatigue and
at very low crack velocity (below 10–10 ms−1), a threshold value of
stress intensity factor (KIo)cyclic of 2.7 MPa m1/2 is observed for cyclic

fatigue suggesting that even under this loading condition which is like
that experienced in patients, quasi infinite lifetimes of this Y-TZP
zirconia ceramic material could be predicted, provided the stress
intensity factor remains lower than the threshold value (K1o)cyclic [420].
The results mentioned above were very promising but as already
mentioned, in 2001, the failure of the zirconia femoral heads (under the
commercial name Prozyr®) led to their withdrawal from the market
and only very few have been used since then, opening the door to the
ZTA composites and also opening a strong and controversial issue on
the future of zirconia as a biomaterial [354].
   Considering that SCG resistance is a critical issue for the long-term
behaviour of ceramic materials, regrettably there is only a sparse
collection of data in the literature concerning ZTA composites [423].
Likewise, a few years ago, in depth research was undertaken on ZTA
ceramics due to the withdrawal of femoral zirconia heads from the
market as well as some issues with alumina. In this context, ZTA
composites can reach superb mechanical properties by paying close
attention to the threshold (KIo) under which no crack KI propagation is
present, since this threshold determines a safety range of use for
orthopaedic applications such as THA. With this purpose, De Aza et al.
[423] investigated slow-crack propagation in ZTA ceramics prepared in
the range 0–15 vol% ZrO2, using powder mixing and a modified
colloidal route. Crack propagation tests were conducted for crack
velocities from 10–12 to 10–2 m/s using the double-torsion technique.
They found that the composites obtained by the colloidal route
exhibited better mechanical properties than those processed by the
powder mixing technique, and more specifically, the composite 10 vol%
of ZrO2 was the best ZTA one processed in their research presenting a
threshold, KIo, significantly higher than monolithic alumina suggesting
that for the same pre-existing defects, this composite is expected to
work at loads two times greater than monolithic alumina without any
delayed failure, so improving the safety range for usage in orthopaedic
implants [408]. In fact, the crack propagation parameter n for this ZTA
composite was 59.6 which is higher than obtained by Lube and Baierl
[413] (n of 32.7) for high purity alumina and that obtained by
Wojteczko et al. [414] (n of 28.30) for 3Y-TZP. Similar research

concerning the SCG of ZTA was carried out by Ramalingam et al. [424]
by means of a dynamic fatigue indentation technique, reporting a crack
propagation parameter n of 93.2 for ZTA (25% ZrO2) which is high and
could be related to both the local residual stress associated with
thermal anisotropies, or alternatively, from the crack tip shielding
mechanism which has been previously observed and reported by
Becher [425] in ZTA ceramics. Following other experimental techniques
to determine the SCG parameter n in ZTA composites, Guiyu et al. [426]
reported an n value of 60 for Al2O3-10% ZrO2 under static fatigue in
air. Basu [404] revealed an n value of 39 for Al2O3-15% ZrO2 using
static fatigue in water, and Barinov et al. [427] by means of dynamic
fatigue without indentation, obtained an n value of 67 for Al2O3-12%
ZrO2 in air. On the other hand, for Al2O3–10 wt. % unstabilised ZrO2,
Szutkowska and Boniecki [428] reported an n parameter of 9.8 ± 6.37
applying Eq. (8.1) and by means of the load–relaxation technique.
Regarding the ZTA counterpart, the SCG investigations for ATZ ceramics
are very scarce. Nevertheless, Kirsten et al. [429] using the ‘‘constant
stressing rate flexural strength’’ test [430, 431], analogous to a previous
study [432], reported an SCG parameter n of 75 for the ATZ composite
80 wt. % 3Y-TZP–20 wt. % Al2O3, which is 80% higher compared to Y-
TZP, concluding that ATZ can be a very interesting composite for THA
applications as well as for dental prostheses [429]. In spite of this
advantage, it is important to remember that a zirconia matrix
composite is very prone to LTD which in turn compromises its
mechanical properties.
   From these results it can be seen that a higher n value can imply
slower degradation strength and a higher remaining strength, resulting
in a longer lifetime. Meanwhile, the value of n for a determined material
may depend in the first instance on the type of test and therefore, the
reason for this dependence may be determined in great measure by the
details of the crack–microstructure interaction, according to Cook et al.
[433], remembering here the basic concept: zirconia in ZTA must
transform under mechanical stresses and this is how the material
works meaning that it is absolutely normal finding transformed
zirconia in retrievals in accordance with a report by Nguyen et al. [434].
This has led to a wide variety of reported n values, even for a ceramic

with the same nominal composition [424], highlighting which of the
parameters, such as chemical species concentration, environment,
temperature, amongst others, must be taken into account for the
evaluation and determination of the SCG parameter n. To judge from
the results reported in the scientific literature on ceramics for THA, and
mentioned here together with those that we have not mentioned but
also exist, everything seems to indicate that today the most efficient
and available ceramic material for THA is BIOLOX®delta (ZTA). Indeed,
in the most recent research carried out by Tateiwa et al. [435], it is
suggested that BIOLOX®delta continues to meet FDA requirements for
minimum strength regardless of the severity of repetitive stress and
hydrothermal ageing. If zirconia transformation (LTD and stresses)
does not affect the surface integrity (extended pull-out, surfaces lifts in
the order of 10 µm, increase wear, etc.) the transformation is good.
According to arthroplasty registries, mixed ceramics show not only a
lower fracture rate, but also a better long-term survival than alumina
which in turn means that zirconia has greatly accomplished its duties.
In another scenario, it is well known that Si3N4 ceramics have been
intensively investigated over the past decade for potential applications
as a high-temperature structural material [436–439]. SCG results in
Si3N4 at room temperature are almost non-existent and only isolated
values have been reported. For example, Lube and Dusza [440]
reported a crack propagation parameter n of 24.4 for a pressure
sintered silicon nitride (GPSSN) containing ∼3 wt. % Al2O3 and ∼3 wt.
% Y2O3 by using static bend loading technique. Xua et al. [441] obtained
an n value of 57.5, by means of three-point bending test for monolithic
α-Si3N4 at ambient temperature. More in-depth studies are needed to
investigate the real feasibility of using Si3N4 in THA bearings since its
true potential lies in high temperature structural applications.

8.2.5 Wear
Ceramics have been introduced as an alternative to Co–Cr/UHMWPE
bearing couples (commonly used) due to their attractive tribological
properties, low friction coefficient as well as low wear rate [442]. It is
well known that the superb advantages of ceramic surfaces in reducing
the wear particle volume in THA have been extensively documented

[273, 443, 444], but even so, the fracture remains a rare but
catastrophic complication [445, 446]. Moreover, the high hardness of
ceramics in general, and specifically of alumina, provides a minimum
wear of the femoral heads and of the cups, allowing a superior surface
quality. On the other hand, the capability of adsorbing polar molecules
such as water and body fluid provides the lubrication between the
ceramic head and the socket.
   In this perspective, it is common to exploit the bearing coupling of
alumina femoral heads articulating against polyethylene, or
alternatively, against alumina monolithic sockets [442]. For the case of
alumina, the failure in its first generation was caused by the absence of
full final density after it was processed, with a fracture rate of 13%
[447]. A second generation introduced in 1980s resulted in higher
density with smaller grain size offering a fracture rate of less than 5%.
Nowadays, a third generation of Al2O3 is available which is
characterised by high purity, full density and finer microstructure,
achieved by doping it with MgO to control the grain growth and
reaching a lower fracture rate of about 0.004–0.015%, taking advantage
of the HIP technique at about 1250 °C [420, 448]. When in the 1980s
aseptic loosening and osteolysis became the main issue in MoP hip
implants, the firsts CoC couples were launched, starting with alumina
and zirconia [449–451]. The major advantages of ceramics promote the
use of CoC bearings as being the best choice for young patients.
Nevertheless, their use is expensive and moreover, implants require an
excellent surgical insertion to preclude chipping of contact surfaces
[452]. It is noteworthy that alumina ceramic bearings have
demonstrated the lowest in vivo wear rates to date of any bearing
combination, highlighting that the same principles of friction and
lubrication reported for MoM bearings are also valid for CoC bearings
[46]. Investigations carried out by Seyyed Hosseinzadeh et al. [46]
revealed that in vitro wear studies of alumina-on-alumina have shown
that there are two wear phases, as follows: (i) The first phase
denominated “run-in” that involves the first million or so cycles where
the volumetric wear rates measured was 0.1 to 0.2 mm3 per million
cycles, and (ii) The second phase called “steady-state” where the
volumetric wear rates is decreased to less than 0.02 mm3 per million
cycles. If these results are compared to MoP couples in the same

phases, the wear is reduced by up to 5000-fold. In other research
works, Affatato et al. [453] demonstrated in their investigations on
alumina vs. Alumina that the wear rate was lower for pure alumina in
comparison to alumina composites without observing significant
differences at a 95% level of confidence. Similarly, Affatato et al. [454]
undertook wear studies on the tribo-behaviour of two different batches
of alumina BIOLOX®forte (28 mm vs. 36 mm) on a hip simulator under
bovine calf serum for five million cycles. The results showed that the
36 mm BIOLOX®forte size showed less weight loss than the 28 mm
BIOLOX®forte size suggesting an influence of the femoral head size on
the tribological properties under specific test conditions. Interesting
work was reported by Nevelos et al. [455] on the behaviour of CoC
bearings carried out with alumina prepared by means of HIP technique
and compared with the standard alumina ones. A reduction of the wear
rate for the HIPed prosthesis when working under standard conditions
was observed, whereas a different behaviour was obtained under
Gelofusione® (4% w/v solution of succinylated gelatine) and water
lubricants, where the standard alumina ceramic showed a lower wear
rate. The author concluded that their results were significantly affected
by uncertainties as testified by the large error bars. On the other hand,
from this study, it is noted that under standard testing conditions, the
wear rates were an order of magnitude lower than the majority of
reported clinical wear rates for in vivo ceramic prostheses, as reported
by Mittelmeier and Heisel [456] and Dorlot et al. [457]. A
representative summary showing the hard bearings wear rates found in
vitro through simulators [452, 458–462] is shown in Table 8.8. Solarino
et al. [463] reported that CoC coupling shows a minimal friction and
wear even with femoral heads larger than 28 and 22.2 mm. Moreover, a
wider range of movement of the artificial joint which persists over the
years, protecting the hip from early or late dislocation, can be reached
with the use of a ball measuring 32 mm or more.

THA, Esposito et al. [464] disclosed the importance of the orientation of
the acetabular component in an alumina-on-alumina hip, inasmuch as
is very likely to have the lowest wear if the acetabular component
orientation satisfies the following formula:



where y is inclination and x is anteversion. Based on this formula,
Esposito et al. [464] pointed out that “the further the result is from 0°,
the greater the chance of high wear. Anteversion is a more important
determinant than inclination for wear in CoC bearing”. Moreover, these
authors found a correlation between anteversion and wear very similar
to that in a previous study by Lusty et al. [465], with a wear rate
associated with anteversion < 15°. Sexton et al. [466] reported high-

acetabular component anteversion is associated with squeaking and
consequently a high wear rate. It is important to stress that the
optimum acetabular position and the relationship between this and the
wear is highly dependent on the patient’s range of movement, which
could be different for each one.

Due to the already mentioned issues presented by alumina and
zirconia monoliths in orthopaedic applications, the best balance
between hardness, toughness and hydrothermal resistance has been
reached thanks to alumina–zirconia composites in order to improve the
ceramic properties [467]. Indeed, in the last fifteen years, the
combination of these mechanical properties has led to the
commercialisation of [215] ZTA composites improving their properties
as a consequence of well dispersed and isolated zirconia grains
constrained in an alumina matrix. Previous works [468, 469], have
experimentally studied the effect of shocks as a source of wear damage
on ZTA hip joints, where shocks are associated with micro-separation,
that is, a separation between the femoral head and cup that induces
short and high contact stresses between those two components at heel-
strike, as pointed out by Dennis et al. [470] and Lombardi et al. [471].
Based on the above mentioned, an interesting investigation was carried
out by Clarke et al. [472] under ‘severe’ micro-separation test mode by
means of a CoC simulator with 36 mm BIOLOX® implants including
ZTA composites (BIOLOX®delta, ‘d’) compared to alumina as the
historical control (BIOLOX®forte, ‘f’). For this, they experimented four
possible combinations (ball-cup: dd, df, fd and ff) which were run
simultaneously in a hip simulator to 5 million cycles duration (5Mc)
with femoral heads of 36 mm diameter. According to Asif [473], “the
micro-separation occurs during the swing phase when the load is
minimal and could occur clinically due to different factors such as head
offset deficiency, laxity of the joint, medialised cup, impingement or
subluxation”. The wear rates for all 36 mm CoC combinations tested by
Clarke et al. [472] were very low, even under the severe micro-
separation test conditions. The ff pairings demonstrated an ‘average’
wear rate of 1.5 mm3/Mc whereas clinical wear rates for contemporary
alumina THA retrievals ranged from 0.1 to 3.6 mm3/year, which is
within the mid-clinical range for alumina implants. The trend in this
investigation was ranked as ff ≫ (df ≥ fd) > dd, in other words, ff pairs
had the highest THA wear rates and dd pairs had the lowest. Likewise,
making comparison between 36 mm versus 28 mm head size, the
results are clinically negligible [472]. On the other hand, the micro-
separation simulation research generated stripe wear on all ceramic
components (BIOLOX®forte, BIOLOX®delta). Perrichon et al. [467]

reported that shocks under micro-separation release wear debris of
various shapes and sizes through inter and intra-granular cracks
affected the hardness of the implant as well as the Young’s modulus.
Studies on ZTA composites have revealed that shocks are the origin of
wear stripes on the femoral head surfaces, and that they have to be
considered in order to reproduce the in vivo degradation. The
successful results with BIOLOX®delta have allowed the production of
larger sized femoral heads with a reduced dislocation rate due to the
reduced impingement and improved stability [474]. The reader is
referred to consult Ref. [473] for a more detailed study of the wear of
ZTA composites.
   Regardless of the drastic slow down after the catastrophic failure of
specific batches of Y-TZP heads in the early 2000s which led to the
premature LTD [467], isolated studies on the wear characteristics and
clinical performance of zirconia femoral heads articulating against
UHMWPE [475] have been reported with some contradictory results,
considering that, as previously mentioned, both zirconia against
alumina and zirconia against zirconia present catastrophic rates of
wear in vitro as reported by Willmann et al. [273]. For example, results
by Stilling et al. [71] do not suggest any advantage of zirconia
articulating against PE compared to CoCr heads, and moreover, they did
not experience zirconia head fractures at midterm follow up. On the
other hand, Hummer et al. [312] and Oldenburg et al. [476], reported
cases of catastrophic results after revision of fractured zirconia ceramic
heads. From many years ago, and more specifically in 1991, a new
product called Hylamer was marketed by DePuy-Dupont Orthopaedics
(Newark, New Jersey) which was expected to have better yield strength
and less wear compared to UHMWPE, to be tested in articulation
against zirconia femoral heads [477, 478]. The annual wear for zirconia
articulating against UHMWPE was 0. 17 mm/year whereas the wear of
zirconia vs Hylamer was 0.40 mm/year [475]. Considering the
conflicting results reported about the performance of the zirconia
femoral head articulating with both UHMWPE and Hylamer, it is
suggested that these femoral heads should not be used in THA. Hylamer
was withdrawn from the market after several studies demonstrated
high rates of wear and revision, according to Livingston et al. [479] and
Cohen [480].

It is well known that a great majority of failures in THA were
strongly related to wear of the cup, head and liner, where the
accumulation of wear particles can be linked to osteolysis which leads
to aseptic implant loosening [481]. However, today with alumina matrix
and Vitamin E-infused highly cross-linked polyethylene (VitE-XLPE),
this is not an issue anymore because Rochcongar et al. [482] reported
results confirming that wear rates were lower in HXLPE/VitE cups than
in UHMWPE cups, suggesting that HXLPE/VitE cups may prevent
osteolysis, implant loosening, and eventually revision surgery. However,
a challenge would be to reduce the generation of wear particles from
the implant surfaces and therefore, Si3N4, which has a low wear rate
when sliding against itself, would probably be in the short term a
possible candidate for THA, emphasising that wear particles of this
non-oxide ceramic can be slowly dissolved in polar liquids with the
potential to be resorbed in vivo so reducing the risk for aseptic
loosening. According to Boshitskaya et al. [483], an advantage of Si3N4
for applications in THA lies in that Si3N4-powders are dissolved in
blood serum and gastric juices which suggests that the use of this
ceramic material in THA may produce less wear particles which in turn
would be biocompatible and biodegradable. Olofsson et al. [481]
concluded that Si3N4 sliding against Si3N4 showed a low wear rate in
bovine serum as well as phosphate buffered saline (PBS). In this
context, this good material combination for THA is promising and
possibly its performance could be much better as a coating on CoCr.
Further investigations are needed with the purpose to know the true
future of Si3N4 as a ceramic material for applications in THA.
Nonetheless, it is very important to point out that there is no need for
new ceramic materials in THA taking into account that ceramics have
shown to be successful in THA and therefore, it is preferable to expand
their use to other applications and to abandon CoCr completely.

8.2.6 Accelerated Ageing Tests
Another problem with the use of zirconia lies in its spontaneous
transformation to its stable monoclinic form under in vivo conditions,
known as LTD [274, 292, 484, 485]. Known about for more than
30 years [486], this results in increased implant surface roughness,

enhanced wear, weakening of the material, and eventual fracture [310,
487]. In simple terms, Y-TZP may perform better than Al2O3 but it is
very sensitive to industrial variations [292]. Thanks to excellent
mechanical properties and tribological performance, ZrO2 was
introduced as an alternative to alumina for the manufacture of femoral
heads [488]. It is worth remembering that ZrO2 exists in three different
forms of crystalline structure: (i) the stable and brittle cubic (c) form at
2370 ºC; (ii) the stable, monoclinic (m) form present at ambient
temperature; and (iii) the hardest and strongest but metastable
tetragonal (t) crystalline form [327, 467, 484, 489, 490]. Although
zirconia can be stabilised with oxides such as yttria [491], ceria,
magnesia or calcia [485], Y-TZP has been used extensively due to its
fine grain size and superb mechanical properties. However, efforts in
developing zirconia-based ceramics with improved reliability for
application in THA seem unsuccessful inasmuch as concerns exist
related to their phase stability, structural reliability, and long-term wear
performance [492, 493]. It is important to note that under thermal or
mechanical stress (stress-induced phase transformation), ZrO2 has the
ability to transform from its metastable t phase at ambient temperature
to its stable m phase, representing one remarkable (somewhat
unexpected) finding in the ceramic field [494, 495]. In fact, in the
1970s, first Garvie et al. [496] and then Gupta et al. [497] showed that
zirconia exhibits a transformation toughening mechanism that acts to
resist crack propagation. The relevance here is that the volume increase
related to the structural differences is the source of increased crack
resistance propagation, partially closing the crack when propagating.
From this discovery, extensive investigations have been developed to
understand the underlying mechanisms and potential implications and
applications of this important phenomenon [495]. Paradoxically, the
mentioned transformation, which imparts high strength and toughness
to the zirconia, can cause a large reduction in strength when this
material is exposed to temperatures in the range of room temperature
to 500 °C for an extended period of time, especially under humid
conditions, which in turn promotes the grains to pop-up and pull-out,
microcrack formation, as well as subsequent surface degradation [484,
495]. Nowadays, the exact mechanism for this LTD is reasonably well

understood but some occasional reports of experimental results do not
seem to support these theories. For example, given enough time, the
degradation can take place at room temperature. It is was
demonstrated that Y-TZP material containing a low (2.5 mol. 9%) yttria
concentration presented spontaneous cracks in a large number of
pieces when these were stored under office conditions for several years
[498]. As a consequence, investigations of the rupture of hip joints
prosthesis caused by the transformation have regained interest from a
biomedical point of view, mainly for ZTA considering that today, pure
zirconia is rarely used in THA.
   The LTD is time dependent [487, 499] in vitro and in vivo [500–
503] occurring as a result of a slow process of t to m phase
transformation of the grains on any surface in contact with water [504]
or body fluids, through the nucleation and growth mechanism of grains
[501]. Clarke et al. [416] argued the ageing kinetics can be sensitive to
different microstructural factors. Moreover, parameters such as purity
of material, yttria content, density, grain size as well as surface
roughness are very important in maintaining the ZrO2 ceramic as Y-
TZP. In fact, the hydrothermal decomposition reaction depends on the
grain size together with distribution of the stabilising yttria within the
zirconia grains [505]. On the other hand, Schubert and Frey [506] and
Chevalier et al. [274] reported that LTD is induced by polar molecules
(typically water) and as a consequence of that, the t phase is
destabilised and transforms to m phase without any external
mechanical stress. Besides, the volume expansion due to the
transformed domains puts the surface of components under
compressive stress leading to the opening up of grain boundaries,
which in turn facilitates the interpenetration of fluid into the bulk of the
material. This LTD phenomenon, along with in vivo failure of ceramic
hip joints, has been the main reason for the downturn of Y-TZP for
applications in THA [494, 507, 508]. Additionally, LTD is typically
described by a nucleation and growth model according to Mehl, Avrami
and Johnson [509, 510].
   In spite of that LTD has not yet been fully understood and the
reported results are not totally in accord with each other, but it is clear
that the t to m phase transformation proceeds from the surface to the
interior [486, 511–513]. Guilardi et al. [514] proved in their

investigations that the t to m phase transformation is a time-dependent
spontaneous mechanism which is accelerated in the presence of
different stimuli (moisture, temperature, mechanical cycling), no
affecting both strength and structural reliability of Y-TZP ceramic
under different experimental regimens carried out in their
investigations. Nonetheless, it must also must be considered that not all
Y-TZP materials behave similarly when submitted to stimuli, insomuch
as they present differences in terms of composition and grain size and
therefore, these are prone to present a high resistance to the effects of
LTD [514, 515]. According to Guo [508], LTD can be delayed by
increasing dopant content, the reduction of grain size, as well as the
creation of an inert surface layer that can be produced by a
recrystallised tetragonal layer with finer grain size [516], or
alternatively, a cubic surface layer [517]. Given around 20 years of
clinical experience related to zirconia femoral heads as well as more
than 600,000 heads implanted, the results about this topic are very
varied, some successful in vivo [518], others with osteolysis and surface
degradation [316, 494], but there are a few reporting degradation by
ageing or LTD [354]. Nonetheless, most investigations on zirconia
implants were processed when the ageing was not yet fully understood.
   Undoubtedly, different investigations have proven that the strength
and fracture toughness of Y-TZP ceramics are dramatically reduced
when they are used in humid environments at temperatures between
150 and 400 °C for long times [519–522]. In fact, Lange et al. [519]
argued that Y2O3 reacts with water to form Y(OH)3 which leads to the
Y2O3 not acting as a stabiliser so favouring the t to m phase
transformation. Considering these arguments as well as the different
typical degradation mechanisms suggested by several researchers, and
reported by Guo [508] in zirconia ceramics, other materials must be
investigated with the purpose to avoid the LTD. Indeed, ZTA ceramics
have replaced previous material generations of monolithic alumina and
zirconia in the ceramic field, as well as cobalt-chrome alloys in metals
[435, 523, 524] for applications in orthopaedics. There are an
important collection of results concerning investigations with ZTA
composites under humid environments [279, 322, 336, 365, 367, 376,
467, 495]. For example, Bartolomé et al. [525] reported significant
ageing (up to 40 vol% m-ZrO2 after 20 h of ageing treatment time) and

microcracking at Al2O3 grain boundaries for ZrO2, higher than the
percolation limit of 16 vol%, creating pathways for water diffusion from
the surface towards the bulk. On the other hand, a homogeneous
distribution of alumina grains act as a constraint to the zirconia grains,
contributing to a high hydrothermal degradation resistance inasmuch
as the t-ZrO2 phase can be retained.
   Reyes-Rojas et al. [526] investigated the ageing applied to Al2O3 + 
13 wt. % Y-TZP + 2 wt.% m-ZrO2 composite in steam at 134 °C under a
pressure of 2 bar. They found that the fraction of monoclinic polymorph
(obtained values by means of Rietveld analysis conducted on the θ–2θ
XRD data) was of 2%, 2.3% and 2.6% for ageing times of 0, 40, and
125 h, respectively, compared to 84.8% for pure Y-TZP aged for 40 h. It
is probable that with a homogeneous dispersion of ZrO2 into the
matrix, the fine grain size, as well as the high Young's modulus of the
Al2O3 matrix, can provide a constraining effect on the zirconia and
could partially inhibit the phase transformation, which is in accordance
with the report by Bartolomé et al. [525]. In other words, the
mentioned homogeneous dispersion of zirconia into the alumina matrix
facilitates the non-propagation of the transformation by the presence of
Al2O3 grains between zirconia ones. This composite, in terms of the
monoclinic phase content, fulfils ISO 1336–2008 requirements for
orthopaedic applications once their mechanical properties are valued.
   Perrichon et al. [467] studied the resulting morphologies and
microstructures of ZTA composites (belonging to the latest generation
of commercialised BIOLOX® delta implants, CeramTec GmbH
(Plochingen, Germany)), after in vitro tests simulated the in vivo
degradation. They focussed on the femoral head inasmuch as an
analysis of the cup can require the development of very specific
characterisation procedures due to its concavity, and visualised that the
presence of both surface and sub-surface micro-cracks triggered the
ZrO2 phase transformation in those worn areas, reducing further crack
propagation which in turn could contribute to the long-term resistance
of the ZTA composite material against hydrothermal ageing. However,
the fact that a moderate increase of the monoclinic fraction after severe
ageing tests is observed does not necessarily mean a decrease in
mechanical properties for this specific type of composite [527], which

today is the bio-ceramic gold standard for load-bearing components in
THA [435]. This emphasises that the early scientific literature
concerning ZTA ageing kinetics indicated that the t to m phase
transformation was also sensitive to both composition and processing,
according to Gutknecht et al. [528]. In spite of several predictions on
LTD under 2 bar applied pressure at 134 °C, as well as controversial
results, some independent research groups have subsequently reported
that ZTA femoral head retrievals showed significantly higher amounts
of polymorphic transformation [529–531] in comparison to reports by
Guicciardi et al. [527], Gaillard et al. [532], and Muñoz-Tabares et al.
[533]. Likewise, a strong increase of the polymorphic transformation of
ZrO2 has been observed [435] in proximity of metal staining [534].
These authors suggested that the hydrogen generated by the reactions
between metal and steam accelerated the flow of water molecules and
free oxygen to vacancy sites in the zirconia lattice [535]. In spite of
everything that happened, an extraordinary balance between SCG and
LTD resistance [363, 490, 494] can be reached with ZTA composites
which offer high mechanical properties and a complete stability for
alternative applications such as knee prostheses or dental implants
[531]. Nonetheless, Yildirim and Kern [536] investigated ZTA
composites with a typical biomedical grade composition [537] and they
revealed that these materials are very sensitive to changes such as
stabiliser composition and sintering conditions, reaching great LTD
resistance with a stabiliser concentration range between 1.1 and 1.2%.
Indeed, almost entirely tetragonal materials with 1.2 and 1.4 mol%
yttria are quite stable with a final monoclinic content < 20% for the
longest exposure time, as can be seen in Fig. 8.11 [536]. Under this
criterion, these ZTA composites can therefore be considered absolutely
safe for THA applications and exposure times in vivo of several decades.
It is worth noting that regardless of the published results on LTD of ZTA
ceramics, the optimum range to obtain an important balance between
good strength, fracture resistance, and sufficient LTD resistance, is very
narrow.

   Given the excellent properties of ZTA ceramics and due to an
increasing interest in aesthetics and concerns originated by toxic and
allergic reactions to certain alloys, both patients and dentists have been
looking for other alternatives. ZTA composites could be candidates for
potential use in dental applications such as endodontic posts, crown
and bridge restorations and implant abutments [538]. Last, but not
least, the dental market is still led by titanium, and ceramics still have
to gain the attention of the majority of dentists. In fact, Aragón-Duarte
et al. [539] reported a monoclinic zirconia phase content of 7% in ZTA
ceramics for dental applications aged under a solution of artificial
saliva at 134 °C and 2 bar pressure, results which are promising for
these applications. Some interesting results related this field are
reported, for example, in [490, 540, 541].
   As was mentioned in Sect. 6.​4, a great challenge lies in being able to
avoid LTD of the zirconia-based composites without compromising

their mechanical properties. In this context, Estili et al. [542] have
reported a content of 55 and 10% of monoclinic ZrO2 in ATZ
composites sintered at the same temperature in an air atmosphere,
using alumina and graphite powder as a powder bed, respectively. The
most interesting and surprising of these results is the formation in-situ
of a surface alumina protective layer (Fig. 6.​7) when it is sintered in a
graphite powder bed, which significantly delays the LTD. The thickness
of the protective alumina layer could be varied considering the final
sintering time. It seems that carbonaceous products could inhibit the
transformation of t to m phase since small addition of MWCNTs to the
ATZ composite (ATZ + 0.01 wt. % MWCNTs) produced a 7% of
monoclinic ZrO2 phase compared to 10% produced by the same ATZ
composite free of MWCNTs, sintered under identical conditions (under
graphite powder bed). More recently, Bocanegra-Bernal et al. [543]
corroborated the in-situ formation of the mentioned alumina layer
surrounding ATZ samples, sintering them for longer times compared to
previous investigations [542, 544] under the presence of graphitic
compounds and a low oxygen atmosphere. The layer formation
mechanism can be due to the reaction of CO with Al2O3 during the
heating stage of the composites, where the formed volatile species of
aluminium in contact with the specimen surface, and owing to the
presence of CO2, are oxidised to the non-volatile Al2O3, thus forming the
surface layer. Undoubtedly, the occurrence of this phenomenon
improves the hydrothermal stability enhancing the possibility of using
ATZ in THA as well as other applications, such as solid oxide fuel cells,
and thermal barrier coatings. Therefore, this new and economical
proposed route can be of vital importance to reach at constant sintering
temperature and different times, the option to in-situ form a dense and
hard alumina protective layer with varied thicknesses which could
avoid the creation of a path for the water to penetrate down into the
specimen. Nevertheless, the most used ceramic material for
orthopaedic applications is still ZTA composite. In fact, Johannes and
Schneider [545] have reported hydrothermal stability in the HIPed ZTA
composite (ZrO2 + 10 wt.% Al2O3) aged at 134 °C in water vapour
under 2 bar pressure, obtaining a monoclinic zirconia phase content of
approximately 1.5% after 192 h in the hydrothermal environment.

They argued that this LTD resistance is due to the small grain size (143 
± 40 nm). The alumina addition stabilises the tetragonal phase and it
could work as a barrier for the propagation of the phase transformation
into the bulk [546, 547]. In spite of successful results, it is generally
necessary to carry out investigations of the LTD of each newly
developed zirconia-based ceramic [547].
     It is noteworthy that in spite of the promising results with respect
to ZTA compounds, there is no doubt that ATZ composites show high
potential for joint replacement applications, since this composite
combines the hardness and wear resistance of alumina as well as the
fracture toughness and biaxial bending strength of zirconia. From this
point of view, a typical surface microstructure for ATZ composite
presents a predominant phase of zirconia surrounded by grains of
alumina (See Fig. 6.​6a). However, for the ATZ composite obtained by
Bocanegra-Bernal et al. [543] in their recent investigations, its typical
microstructural surface comprises an alumina protective layer which
covers all the surface of the ATZ composite into an “alumina” monolith
with the excellent properties of zirconia (See Fig. 6.​6b), so avoiding the
water penetration into the bulk of ATZ composite and improving the
LTD. However, strong investigations are needed in order to evaluate the
mechanical properties before and after ageing tests. Really, the report
concerning the LTD of ZTA highlights the reduced roughening of ZTA
compared to Y-TZP [489, 526, 548] so corroborating the few available
studies on explanted ZTA components that specifically examine this
point, according to Gremillard et al. [549]. On the other hand, the
reported scientific literature on LTD of ATZ composites is even less
extensive and therefore, papers detailing the LTD on explanted ATZ
femoral heads are non-existent. Conversely, literature can be found that
refers to flat samples that at no time perfectly reproduce the final
surface characteristics of implanted components such as roughness and
residual stresses [548]. Regardless of numerous differences reported
regarding materials for applications in orthopaedics by scientists,
industrialists and especially, orthopaedic surgeons, zirconia-based
ceramics [354] are the most important of them since it was introduced
20 years ago to solve the brittleness, as well as the potential failure of
implants [550]. However, for the short and middle term it seems that a
combination of Al2O3 and ZrO2 can lead to the production of an

advanced composite optimising the manufacturing processes and raw
materials in order to get the best properties. The study and
understanding of the LTD, which is considered the Achilles heel of these
alumina–zirconia composites in orthopaedic applications is of
paramount importance for long-term performance of THA.

and Technologies

It is well known that metals and their alloys, ceramics and polymers
have been extensively used as biomaterials in joint replacements. Given
the different atomic arrangement in these materials, there are a wide
range of physical, mechanical, and chemical properties. However,
although many of them have been manufactured in the industry, only
some can be used in the orthopaedic field, and more specifically in THA,
due to their bioactive, bio inert or biodegradable properties, as well as
attractive mechanical properties such as strength, stiffness, fatigue life
and so forth [1–4]. For the case of metals, these properties are strongly
governed by their composition, microstructure, and phases and

therefore, considering these different properties they could provide
different applications in orthopaedics [2]. Regardless of whether it is a
metal, ceramic or polymer, the main goal in THA is to return a patient to
activities of daily living and a range of motion in the absence of pain as
soon as possible and thus, in order to achieve that goal, a constant
development of the material candidates to be used in joint replacement
is essential [1]. According to Yoruc and Şener [4], Miura et al. [5] and
Guo et al. [6], the new developments in artificial hip joints are
essentially focussed on mechanical strength, biocompatibility,
bioactivity and alternative materials that can impart better wear
resistance and mechanical reliability [7]. It is important to understand
that THA is formed by two components: on the one hand a cup type and
on the other a long femoral type where the head of the femoral element
fits inside the cup enabling the articulation of the joint. For many years,
these two parts have been fabricated from metals, ceramics, polymers,
and composites. The use of polymeric materials only results in a very
fragile structure not suitable to meet the requirement of stress
deformation responses in THR components [8]. On the other hand,
although metals possess extraordinary mechanical properties, their
biocompatibility is poorer inasmuch as the release of dangerous metal
ions leads to detrimental consequences, like eventual failure, and in
many cases to the removal of the implant. In view of these unfortunate
events, ceramic materials such as alumina and zirconia which usually
have excellent biocompatibility but poor fracture toughness, being
prone to be brittle, have emerged. However, a combination of these two
monoliths have led to the fabrication of ZTA and ATZ composites where
ZTA is the more established material for THA taking advantage of the
combination of its biocompatibility, mechanical strength, and
toughness [9]. In fact, the current challenge is focussed on several
studies leading to obtain a perfect balance of properties, the result of an
interdisciplinary research involving a great effort of material scientists,
biomedical specialists, pathologists and clinicians, aimed at producing
an implant to serve for longer times without rejection [8]. Nowadays,
the scientific literature reveals that the main materials used in THAs are
titanium, cobalt-chromium, PE, and ceramics, respectively [1].
Moreover, when we mention THA there are several options from which

to choose the bearing surface, such as CoC, CoP, MoP, each with its
advantages and drawbacks [10].
     It is also clear that the use of MoM hip resurfacing implants should
be made taking into account the pros and cons, considering relevant
factors such as age, gender, body size, physical fitness and lifestyle,
being that MoM pose the highest risk of provoking undesirable allergic
reactions, and if MoM is the best fit for a patient’s needs, the surgery
must be carried out by an expert orthopaedic surgeon to minimise the
risks [11]. On the other hand, when ceramics are used, there is a very
rare risk for fracture whereas metal bearings cannot fracture but are
more prone to loosen and could require a second (revision) surgery. In
another scenario, MoM releases tiny particles of metal into the joint
which is absent with ceramics. However, in the event that ceramic
debris can occur, the body does not seem to react to these wear
particles like it does to the less biocompatible metal debris. The
orthopaedic community is inclined to use metal bearings with
polyethylene liners in older, less active individuals who are going to
want this surgery to be their last. When it comes to younger and more
active patients, the choice of the best bearing must be decided on a case
by case basis where both surgeon and patient should consider all the
pros and cons of the different articulating options (MoM resurfacing
only, CoP, CoC, MoP) according to age, activity level, bone density and
seriously comparing the relative risks and advantages offered by MoM
and CoC options, the most commonly used nowadays. The use of MoP
for younger patients is getting rare. The potential complications and
every effort made to prevent any anticipated problems must also be
considered [12, 13].
   To ensure implant longevity in THA, an improvement in the
manufacturing process, raw materials, and testing methods in vitro that
can yield almost the same results as in vivo, undoubtedly lead towards
the attainment of these goals. Thus, the scientific community will need
to focus on not only further reducing abrasive wear, but also on
reducing stress shielding by newer materials, as well as new designs.
Although this is not an issue at all, the near future target, which is
becoming a business need, will be substituting CoCr in other
applications. Ceramics should win over alternative materials such as
poly-ether-ether-ketone (PEEK). In closing, a wide and comprehensive

knowledge of the characteristics, advantages and disadvantages of each
bearing surface is of paramount importance for the surgeon’s group
who routinely perform THA. Likewise, personnel with high experience
will help in selecting the best coupling for each patient with the unique
purpose of providing the best long-term survivorship of the prosthesis,
emphasising once again that the best option according to the latest
technological advances can be CoC in young and active patients [10].

Joint replacement using different materials has been used over the past
50 years with outstanding success. Millions of people throughout the
world have benefited from THA surgery, extending their mobility and
quality-of-life by years. However, a clear conclusion can be the one
reported by Kuncická et al. [1] who points out that “significant
opportunities remain to improve joint replacements by improving the
materials from which they are made. While metals, ceramics, and
polymers each serve critical functions in implant systems, their respective
roles and properties are shifting with the advancements in each category
and the introduction of hybrid material systems”. After reviewing
different metallic, ceramic, polymeric and composite materials used
nowadays in THA, there remain issues that must be solved in order to

ensure good pain relief, increasing more and more the activity levels in
young patients undergoing hip replacement, as well as a longevity of
the prosthesis, reaching a higher range of motion as well as a stability
in those ranges. It was observed that the mechanical, material and
processing issues are imperative in the design, selection and
improvement in the fabrication of hip replacements. For the specific
application such as THA, a correct choice of the specific material to
fulfil the requirements of different standards for particular orthopaedic
applications is necessary. The proper selection of metallic, ceramic,
polymeric or composite material plays a crucial role for getting the
combination of properties such as high strength, wear, and corrosion
resistance, as well as biocompatibility. With the passage of time and
balancing the pros and cons of the various materials used for
applications in THA, it could be determined that the use of ceramic
materials (alumina and ZTA composite mainly) is best suited to these
types of applications. In closing, the innovations in the design and
fabrication processes for the different materials for THA are raising the
great reality of being able to obtain, in the medium term, implants with
improved performance to match both the biocompatibility and
mechanical complexity of the hip implants. However, to achieve this,
surgeons in close alliance with biologists and engineers cannot be
ignored and therefore, must be persuaded with the long-term
durability and reliability of the available biomaterials. Everything
mentioned leads in the future to see novel biomaterials being
developed that will increase the lifespan of orthopaedic implants.
Today it is not possible to fully ensure which material is definitely the
one that will dominate orthopaedics.
